lessons.unit: Unit 1: Paper 2 Section A - Reading non-fiction (Q1-Q4)
lessons.title: Paper 2 overview and Question 1: true statements
objectives: Describe the structure and marks of AQA Paper 2
Select four true statements accurately for Question 1
Distinguish fact, opinion and half-true distractors

keywords.def: a statement that can be proved true or false
a personal view or belief
a statement that looks right but contains a detail that is wrong
real-life writing such as letters, diaries or memoir that uses literary techniques

starter: Define 'inference' and give an example from a text you know.
Is this a fact or an opinion? 'The school library is the best room in the building.'
Name the five questions on Paper 1 and their marks.

teach.heading: Paper 2 at a glance
bullets: Writers' Viewpoints and Perspectives: 1 hour 45 minutes, 80 marks
Section A: two linked non-fiction sources, Questions 1-4, 40 marks
Section B: one viewpoint writing task, Question 5, 40 marks
One source is 19th century; the other is 20th or 21st century
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Show the sections and note that the sources share a theme. Q1 is 4 marks, Q2 8, Q3 12, Q4 16, Q5 40. Ask: which question carries the same weight as the whole of Section A? Q5. Both need practice.

teach.heading: Question 1: choose four true statements
bullets: Eight statements are given; four are true
Based on a named part of Source A
Shade or tick only the four that are definitely true
One mark for each correct choice
teach.note: Stress careful reading: a statement can be mostly true but contain one wrong detail (for example 'a term' instead of 'a week'). Advise pupils to check each against the text, underlining the matching words.

teach.heading: Fact, opinion and traps
bullets: Check names, numbers, time and place in each statement
Watch for words like always, never, all, only
Do not use outside knowledge, only the text
If it is not in the lines, it cannot be true here
teach.note: Show a trap: text says 'three students borrowed the same novel'. A statement 'Many students borrowed the same novel' is looser; discuss whether it is true. For safety, pupils choose only statements that exactly match.

teach.heading: Worked example
bullets: Source A: a school trialled a phone-free week
True: the library queue got longer
False: the corridors became quieter
False: everyone was convinced
teach.note: Teacher-written Source A: 'Last term our school trialled a phone-free week. By Wednesday, the corridors were louder, the library queue was longer and three students had borrowed the same novel. Teachers reported that pupils looked up more often. Not everyone was convinced: one Year 10 told me, grumpily, that she felt 'cut off from the entire world'. I confess I felt the same on Monday morning.' Work through slowly.

teach.heading: Reading two sources
bullets: Read the question first to know the focus
Skim both sources for gist and writer's attitude
Note the date and form of each source
Use about 15 minutes of reading time in total
teach.note: Explain that Paper 2 has more reading than Paper 1 and the two sources are linked by topic. The date matters: the 19th-century source will have older vocabulary and sentence structure.

practice: Using the phone-free week extract, decide whether each statement is true or false: (1) The school trialled a phone-free week. (2) The trial lasted a whole term. (3) By Wednesday the corridors were quieter. (4) The library queue grew longer. (5) Three students borrowed the same novel. (6) Teachers said pupils looked up more often. (7) Everyone was convinced. (8) The writer felt cut off from the world on Friday.
Rewrite statement 8 so that it becomes true.
independent: For each false statement in the practice (2, 3, 7, 8), underline the exact words in the extract that prove it false.
Write two statements of your own about the extract: one true, one a convincing distractor.
Explain why 'The writer enjoyed the phone-free week' cannot be chosen as true.
exit: State two checks you should make on each Question 1 statement.
Is 'Everyone was convinced' fact or opinion? Explain.
lessons.homework: Read a short newspaper or magazine article and write eight statements about it, four true and four false, for a partner to mark.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: give the extract with line numbers and a table for T/F plus evidence. Stretch: construct distractors that change only one detail and explain what you changed.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Paper 2 Section A - Reading non-fiction (Q1-Q4)
lessons.title: Question 2: summarising differences between two sources
objectives: Understand what Question 2 asks and how it is marked
Synthesise points from both sources into a clear summary
Use inference and comparison connectives

keywords.def: combine information from two sources into one clear point
a brief account of the main points
a word that links ideas, such as whereas or in contrast
work out an idea from clues in the text

starter: How many marks is Question 1 and how many statements are true?
Write one fact and one opinion about your school.
Give a connective of contrast.

teach.heading: What Question 2 asks
bullets: 8 marks, AO1: identify and interpret explicit and implicit information
Uses both sources
Asks for a summary of the differences between them on a given focus
Spend about 10 minutes
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Show a typical stem: 'You need to refer to Source A and Source B for this question. Use details from both sources to write a summary of the differences between...' Emphasise 'differences', not similarities, and 'summary', not analysis.

teach.heading: Source B for comparison
bullets: A 19th-century voice: formal, opinionated, nostalgic
Young people are called idle and badly behaved
Strict discipline from the writer's boyhood is praised
Compare against Source A on pupils and behaviour
teach.note: Teacher-written Source B (19th-century style): 'It is a lamentable circumstance that the young people of this present age, being furnished with every idle amusement, can scarcely be persuaded to sit an hour with a book. In my own boyhood, we were rapped sharply upon the knuckles for any lapse of attention, and I am bound to say that I learned my letters the faster for it.' Read it twice and unpick difficult words.

teach.heading: Method: point by point
bullets: Choose three or four clear differences
For each, give Source A then Source B
Link with 'whereas', 'but', 'in contrast'
Use brief evidence and your own words
teach.note: Model the grid on screen: Row 1 attitude to pupils; Row 2 discipline; Row 3 effect of change/amusement. Remind pupils not to analyse language in Q2: that belongs to Q3.

teach.heading: Include inferences
bullets: Explicit: Source B says pupils are idle
Inference: B's writer believes the past was better
Explicit: Source A notes pupils 'looked up more often'
Inference: A's writer is mildly positive but unsure
teach.note: Higher bands reward inferences. Ask pupils what a phrase such as 'I am bound to say' implies about Source B's writer (confident, certain, a little proud). Warn against over-quoting.

teach.heading: Model answer
bullets: Source A: a modern writer reports both gains and frustrations
Source B: a Victorian-style writer condemns young people outright
Source A: staff observe more attention, whereas B blames amusements
B praises punishment; A shows no physical punishment
teach.note: Model paragraph: 'Source A presents a school experiment in which pupils become more attentive, whereas Source B suggests that young people are naturally distracted and need strict discipline. In A the writer is open-minded and admits to feeling frustrated himself; in B the writer is certain the past was better, implying that he disapproves of modern youth.'

practice: Fill in a three-row grid comparing Source A and Source B on (a) how young people behave, (b) the writer's attitude, (c) what is said about attention.
Rewrite this weak sentence as a Q2 point: 'Source A is modern and Source B is old.'
independent: Write a full Q2 answer (about 10 minutes): 'Use details from both sources to write a summary of the differences between how young people are viewed in Source A and Source B.'
Highlight two inferences in your answer.
Underline each connective you used.
exit: Give two connectives for showing difference.
Why should you not analyse language in Question 2?
lessons.homework: Write a second version of your answer that adds two further differences, keeping each point to one clear sentence.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: give a word bank for Source B (lamentable, idle, rapped) and a sentence frame ('In Source A..., whereas in Source B...'). Stretch: add an inference about the writer's purpose.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Paper 2 Section A - Reading non-fiction (Q1-Q4)
lessons.title: Question 2: practice with a new pair of sources
objectives: Apply the Q2 method to unfamiliar sources
Write a developed, accurate summary of differences
Check answers against the mark scheme descriptors

keywords.def: a writer's viewpoint or way of seeing a subject
a difference that is clear when two things are set side by side
correct and supported by the text
clear and brief, without waste

starter: Define 'synthesise' in your own words.
Give a connective for difference and one for similarity.
Rewrite in your own words: 'A man eats a sandwich with the concentration of a surgeon.'

teach.heading: Two new sources: transport
bullets: Source C: a modern commuter on a crowded train
Source D: a 19th-century traveller on their first railway journey
Task: differences in how travellers feel and behave
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Teacher-written Source C: 'The 7.42 to Leeds is a metal tube of strangers, every one of us pretending the others do not exist. Headphones go in; eyes drop to screens. A man opposite eats a sandwich with the concentration of a surgeon. We are travelling at ninety miles an hour and nobody has looked out of the window once.' Source D is on the next slide.

teach.heading: Source D
bullets: A 19th-century traveller describes real alarm
The carriage shakes; the engine screams
Other passengers react loudly
The writer avoids looking at the scene
teach.note: Teacher-written Source D: 'I must confess that my first journey upon the railway was attended by considerable alarm. The carriage shook; the engine screamed; and when informed that we were travelling at near twenty miles in the hour, a stout lady beside me begged for her salts. For my own part, I resolved to keep my eyes fixed upon the floor.' Check difficult words: attended, salts.

teach.heading: Spot the differences
bullets: C: speed is ordinary; D: speed is frightening
C: passengers ignore one another; D: passengers react openly
C: people look at screens; D: the writer looks at the floor
Both: people avoid looking at the journey itself
teach.note: Elicit that there is also a similarity (nobody looks out of the window / eyes on the floor), but Q2 wants differences. Use the grid to organise. Ask which differences are explicit and which require inference.

teach.heading: Quality checks
bullets: Is every point supported by a detail from the text?
Have you used both sources in every point?
Have you inferred as well as quoted?
Is your language clear and economical?
teach.note: Share a short model for C and D, then ask pupils to mark it against these four checks. Point out the importance of keeping answers focused on the stem.

practice: Underline two differences between Source C and Source D and note the quotation that proves each.
Write one comparative sentence using 'whereas' for the differences in how speed is experienced.
independent: Timed Q2 (10 minutes): 'Use details from both sources to write a summary of the differences between the travellers' experiences in Source C and Source D.'
Add one inference about each writer's attitude.
Use the four quality checks to mark your own answer and fix one weakness.
exit: What is the main focus word in Q2, similarity or difference?
Write one sentence of inference about Source D's writer.
lessons.homework: Rewrite your Q2 answer in 120 words or fewer without losing the main differences.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a pre-filled grid with line references and a vocabulary list with pictures. Stretch: write a third paragraph that infers what each writer's perspective reveals about the age they live in.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Paper 2 Section A - Reading non-fiction (Q1-Q4)
lessons.title: Question 3: analysing language in non-fiction
objectives: Understand how Question 3 differs from Question 2
Analyse word choices, techniques and sentence forms in non-fiction
Write an analytical paragraph with strong evidence and effect

keywords.def: the attitude a writer conveys, for example humorous or serious
writing using I and we
a word that describes how an action is done
level of formality in language

starter: Name two features of a strong Q2 answer.
What does the adverb 'grumpily' tell us about the Year 10 pupil?
Define connotation.

teach.heading: What Question 3 asks
bullets: 12 marks, AO2: language analysis of one source
How does the writer use language to achieve their purpose?
Only the named source and often a named section
Aim for about 15 minutes and 3-4 analytical points
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Contrast with Q2: Q2 is about content; Q3 is about how the writer uses words. Q3 carries 12 marks, so developed analysis matters. Pupils lose marks for retelling content.

teach.heading: The non-fiction toolkit
bullets: Tone: humorous, confessional, formal, urgent
Person: 'I' creates intimacy and honesty
Rhetorical features: lists, questions, direct address
Word choice: verbs, adverbs and emotive adjectives
teach.note: Link to Source A: 'I confess I felt the same on Monday morning.' Ask what 'I confess' does: it admits a weakness and builds trust. Contrast with the imaginary alternative 'I felt the same.'

teach.heading: Model analysis: Source A
bullets: Point: the writer adopts an honest, light-hearted tone
Evidence: 'I confess'
Analysis: the verb is confessional and slightly comic
Effect: the reader trusts and warms to the writer
teach.note: Read the model aloud and annotate. Then ask what 'grumpily' adds: it makes the pupil's reaction comic, but also shows the writer is gently teasing, not cruel. Tone often depends on small adverbs.

teach.heading: Sentence forms in non-fiction
bullets: Colon: introduces the sting 'Not everyone was convinced:'
Short, direct sentences can make a point land
Lists give pace and variety
Always link the form to its effect
teach.note: Look at the colon in the extract: it sets up a contrast. Ask pupils what the reader expects after a colon. This kind of comment is credit-worthy because it links punctuation to meaning.

teach.heading: Putting it together
bullets: Choose four quotations from different parts of the section
Name the technique and word class precisely
Explain connotations and the effect on the reader
Link each point to the writer's viewpoint
teach.note: Pupils draft a plan: four rows with quotation, technique, effect. Keep an eye on timings. Emphasise the question word 'how' rather than 'what'.

practice: Using Source A (phone-free week), explain what the phrase 'cut off from the entire world' suggests about the pupil's attitude.
Write one point on the colon in 'Not everyone was convinced:' and what it does for the reader.
independent: Q3: How does the writer use language to show his attitude towards the phone-free week? Write three paragraphs in 12-15 minutes.
Annotate: underline a quotation, circle a technique name, and star the effect sentence in each paragraph.
Write one sentence about the final sentence of Source A: 'I confess I felt the same on Monday morning.'
exit: Name two features of a good Q3 paragraph.
What does a confessional tone do to the reader?
lessons.homework: Find a short opinion article online or in a newspaper and write one Q3-style paragraph on a single quotation.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: supply a three-column table (quotation, technique, effect) and a word bank of tone words. Stretch: comment on how tone shifts across the extract.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Paper 2 Section A - Reading non-fiction (Q1-Q4)
lessons.title: Question 3: decoding 19th-century non-fiction
objectives: Decode unfamiliar vocabulary and long sentences
Identify the tone and attitude of a 19th-century writer
Write language analysis on an older text with confidence

keywords.def: serious, polite, elaborate language
old-fashioned and no longer in common use
a sentence with a main clause and one or more subordinate clauses
a feeling that something is wrong or unacceptable

starter: Define 'register'.
Give two techniques a writer might use to sound serious.
What does 'lamentable' suggest, from its sound or context?

teach.heading: Why older texts feel hard
bullets: Longer sentences with several clauses
Words we no longer use every day
Formal, sometimes pompous, tone
Different ideas about what is polite or normal
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Reassure pupils: the exam never asks about historical facts, only about the language. Encourage them to read in small chunks and trust context.

teach.heading: Strategies for decoding
bullets: Look at the context for clues
Break long sentences at semi-colons and commas
Look for a root or a word you already know
Ask: is the tone positive or negative?
teach.note: Practise on Source B: 'lamentable' (suggests sorrow or complaint), 'idle amusements' (pointless entertainments), 'rapped sharply' (hit). Ask pupils for a modern paraphrase of the whole first sentence.

teach.heading: Analysing Source B
bullets: 'Lamentable circumstance' shows strong disapproval
'Idle amusement' dismisses modern pleasures
'I am bound to say' sounds certain and a little proud
Long sentences give an authoritative, lecturing tone
teach.note: Link each to its effect on the reader. A modern reader may find the writer pompous, a fellow Victorian might find him sensible. Mention that both responses are valid as long as they are supported.

teach.heading: Write the analysis
bullets: Point: the writer sounds disapproving and nostalgic
Evidence: 'lamentable circumstance'
Analysis: formal noun phrase signals shock and sadness
Effect: the reader sees him as stern and old-fashioned
teach.note: Model one paragraph and invite pupils to improve it by adding a second quotation. Insist on specific word-class comments (adjective, noun, modal verb).

teach.heading: Sentence structure as evidence
bullets: Semi-colon links the engine and the shaking carriage
A long sentence can build to a climax
A short final sentence can reveal an attitude
Comment on rhythm as well as meaning
teach.note: Use Source D from Lesson 3: 'The carriage shook; the engine screamed;' The semi-colons link two events and speed up the sense of alarm; the personification 'screamed' makes the machine sound like a living thing.

practice: Paraphrase Source B's first sentence in your own modern words.
Explain in two sentences what 'a stout lady beside me begged for her salts' reveals about the writer's view of the lady.
independent: Q3 (15 minutes): How does the writer of Source D use language to describe the first railway journey? Write three analytical paragraphs.
Pick one word you decoded using context and explain how you worked it out.
Write one sentence comparing the tone of Source D with the tone of Source C (preparation for Q4).
exit: Name one strategy for decoding unfamiliar vocabulary.
How can a long sentence affect the tone of a 19th-century text?
lessons.homework: Find a short extract from a Victorian letter or diary in a library or online, paraphrase it, and underline three words that show the writer's attitude.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: pre-teach a glossary (lamentable, alarm, salts) with images and give a split-sentence version of Source D. Stretch: analyse how humour appears in Source D despite the formal tone.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Paper 2 Section A - Reading non-fiction (Q1-Q4)
lessons.title: Question 4: comparing perspectives and methods
objectives: Understand the demands of Question 4 (16 marks)
Compare perspectives and the methods that convey them
Structure a comparative answer clearly

keywords.def: a writer's viewpoint, attitude and feelings about a subject
a language or structural technique a writer uses
that sets two things side by side to show likeness or difference
place close together for contrast

starter: Define perspective in your own words.
Give one example of a language method and one of a structural method.
Name two connectives of comparison.

teach.heading: What Question 4 asks
bullets: 16 marks, AO3: compare writers' ideas and perspectives
Compare how the writers convey their different perspectives
Uses both sources in full
Spend about 20 minutes
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Show the typical stem: 'Compare how the two writers convey their different perspectives and feelings about X. In your answer, you should compare their different perspectives, compare the methods they use to convey their perspectives, support your response with references to both texts.' Underline the three bullet points.

teach.heading: Perspective plus method
bullets: Perspective: what the writer thinks and feels about the topic
Method: how language and structure show this
Strong answers move from idea to method to effect
Compare throughout; avoid two separate essays
teach.note: Model with Sources A and B on attitudes to young people: A is tentative, humorous and balanced; B is certain, severe and nostalgic. Methods: confessional first person versus formal declarative statements.

teach.heading: A comparative paragraph
bullets: Source A's writer is open-minded: 'I confess'
Source B's writer is certain: 'I am bound to say'
Both use the first person but for different effects
A builds trust; B asserts authority
teach.note: Model aloud: 'In Source A the writer's perspective is balanced, shown by the confessional 'I confess', whereas Source B's writer is certain and judgemental, shown by the forceful 'I am bound to say'. Both use first person, but A uses it to build rapport and B to assert authority.' Underline comparative links.

teach.heading: Comparative connectives and structure
bullets: Whereas, while, similarly, in contrast, unlike
Alternate Source A and Source B inside each paragraph
Begin with an overview comparing the two perspectives
Finish with a short judgement of how methods differ
teach.note: Offer a plan: intro (overview), para 1 (attitude to young people), para 2 (tone and sentence structure), para 3 (word choice), conclusion (optional). Emphasise equal coverage of both sources.

teach.heading: Common mistakes
bullets: Writing about one source then the other with no links
Listing techniques without effects
Forgetting to compare perspectives, not just topics
Running out of time on the second source
teach.note: Ask pupils to spot which mistake is shown in a short weak response: 'Source A uses a colon. Source B uses semi-colons.' Rebuild it with them.

practice: Write one comparative sentence using 'whereas' that compares how Source A and Source B treat discipline or attention.
Pick one quotation from each source and say what perspective each conveys.
independent: Plan a Q4 answer: 'Compare how the two writers convey their different perspectives and feelings about young people.' Use a three-paragraph plan with quotations from both sources.
Write the first comparative paragraph with at least two connectives.
Add a second paragraph focusing on a sentence-form method in each source.
exit: What two things must a Q4 answer compare?
Name two comparative connectives.
lessons.homework: Complete your Q4 answer for homework with a short concluding sentence on how the methods differ.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a two-column grid (Source A/Source B) and comparative sentence frames. Stretch: add a comment on how the dates of the sources influence their methods.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Paper 2 Section A - Reading non-fiction (Q1-Q4)
lessons.title: Question 4: writing a full comparative answer
objectives: Write a full timed Q4 response
Embed quotations from both sources
Use level descriptors to evaluate and improve the answer

keywords.def: a short opening statement that sums up the main comparison
a quotation woven into your own sentence
to communicate an idea or feeling
showing deep and insightful understanding

starter: State the two things Q4 asks you to compare.
Write a comparative sentence using 'unlike'.
Turn this into an embedded quotation: the writer says 'idle amusement'.

teach.heading: Timing a Q4 answer
bullets: 2 minutes: reread the key lines of both sources
3 minutes: plan three points with quotations
13 minutes: write three comparative paragraphs
2 minutes: check quotations and spelling
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Explain that today is a timed write on Sources C and D (the railway pair). Pupils may need to scroll between texts. Set a visible timer.

teach.heading: A strong opening
bullets: Name both writers' main perspectives
Show an overview of difference
Mention a key method in each source
Avoid copying the question word for word
teach.note: Model: 'The writer of Source C views the modern commute as lonely and mechanical, whereas the writer of Source D views early rail travel as exciting yet frightening. C relies on a wry list-like tone, while D uses vivid verbs and emotive vocabulary.'

teach.heading: Developing paragraph 1
bullets: Idea: C is cynical about silent travellers
Quotation: 'a metal tube of strangers'
Method: the metaphor dehumanises the train
Compare: D's 'screamed' makes the engine alive
teach.note: Annotate how the model alternates between sources. Check that pupils name a technique and its effect, not just identify it.

teach.heading: Self-assess against levels
bullets: Level 4: perceptive comparison with a detailed range of examples
Level 3: clear comparison with relevant methods
Level 2: some comparison, some methods
Check: do I compare methods, not just ideas?
teach.note: Share the descriptors in simplified form. After writing, pupils highlight comparison in one colour and method in another to see imbalance.

practice: Orally rehearse your opening overview sentence for Sources C and D.
Choose one quotation from each source that will anchor your answer.
independent: Timed (about 20 minutes): 'Compare how the two writers convey their different perspectives and feelings about travelling by train.' Use Sources C and D from Lesson 3.
Highlight comparison words in one colour and methods in another.
Set one target: what will you do differently next time?
exit: What is the purpose of an overview in Q4?
Write one comparative connective you used well.
lessons.homework: Rewrite your weakest paragraph, adding one embedded quotation from each source and a method for each.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: give an annotated model answer and a paragraph frame; allow notes in a table. Stretch: integrate a short evaluative phrase about which writer is more convincing.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Paper 2 Section B - Viewpoint writing (Q5)
lessons.title: Question 5: audience, purpose and form
objectives: Understand how Q5 is marked and what it demands
Identify audience, purpose and form from a task
Use the conventions of letters, articles and speeches

keywords.def: the people who will read or hear your writing
why you are writing: to argue, persuade, explain or advise
the type of text: letter, article, speech, essay
your opinion on a topic, argued with evidence

starter: Define perspective and give an example.
Name two comparative connectives.
Which text type might you use to speak to a large group: a letter or a speech?

teach.heading: What Question 5 asks
bullets: 40 marks: 24 for content and organisation, 16 for technical accuracy
You write a text expressing a point of view on a topic
Spend about 45 minutes, including planning and proofreading
Often linked to the theme of the reading sources
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Show a sample task: ''Young people spend too much time on screens.' Write an article for your school magazine in which you explain your point of view.' Ask: who is the audience? What is the purpose? What form?

teach.heading: Audience and register
bullets: Peers: friendly, but still controlled and Standard English
Headteacher or editor: formal and respectful
Wider public: authoritative and measured
Match vocabulary and sentence length to the audience
teach.note: Rewrite 'screens are rubbish' for a headteacher: 'Excessive screen use can undermine concentration and wellbeing.' Show how register changes without losing the viewpoint.

teach.heading: Form conventions
bullets: Letter: address, greeting, sign-off matched to formality
Article: headline, subheading, strong opening paragraph
Speech: direct address, rhythm, clear signposting
Essay: clear introduction, argument and conclusion
teach.note: Show quick examples: 'Dear Sir or Madam... Yours faithfully'; 'Dear Mrs Rahman... Yours sincerely'; 'Assalamu alaykum, everyone, and good morning' for a school assembly if appropriate. Remind pupils that form earns credit under audience and purpose, but must not take over the argument.

teach.heading: Build a viewpoint
bullets: Decide your stance and keep it consistent
Choose three strong supporting points
Add one counter-argument to answer
Plan an effective hook and a closing call to action
teach.note: Demonstrate a plan for the screens task: hook (anecdote about a quiet dinner table), point 1 (sleep), point 2 (concentration), point 3 (real friendship), counter-argument (learning online), conclusion (a challenge to readers).

teach.heading: Quick audit
bullets: Who am I writing to?
Why am I writing?
What form is this?
How formal should I sound?
teach.note: Ask pupils to complete the audit for two new tasks: (a) a letter to a local councillor about a youth centre, (b) a speech to Year 7 about kindness. Collect answers and correct vague ones.

practice: For each task, state audience, purpose and form: (a) a letter to a newspaper about litter in your area; (b) a speech to parents about homework; (c) an article for teenagers about sleep.
Write an opening sentence for the screens article that would hook a school-magazine reader.
independent: Plan an article: ''Young people spend too much time on screens.' Write an article for your school magazine explaining your point of view.' Include stance, three points, one counter-argument and an ending.
Write the headline and the first paragraph (about 80 words).
Underline the words that show your audience and purpose.
exit: Name the three things to identify before writing Q5.
How would you change the register for a letter to a headteacher?
lessons.homework: Write a complete plan and the first two paragraphs of a letter to your local council arguing for a new place for young people to meet.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a planning grid and form checklists with sample openings; allow bullet-point plans. Stretch: write a hook in two different registers and explain which suits the audience better.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Paper 2 Section B - Viewpoint writing (Q5)
lessons.title: Question 5: persuasive and rhetorical techniques
objectives: Identify and use rhetorical devices accurately
Choose devices that match audience and purpose
Avoid overloading writing with techniques

keywords.def: a question asked for effect, not for an answer
words chosen to provoke feelings
a short personal story that illustrates a point
three linked words or phrases for rhythm and emphasis

starter: State the three things to identify before writing Q5.
Give one example of emotive language about litter.
What is a counter-argument?

teach.heading: The DAFOREST toolkit
bullets: Direct address, Alliteration, Facts, Opinion
Rhetorical question, Emotive language, Statistics, Triples
A memory aid, not a checklist to tick off
Use each device for a reason
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Present DAFOREST as a memory aid. Emphasise that examiners reward sustained, purposeful persuasion, not a list of tricks. Add anecdote and repetition as extra tools.

teach.heading: Examples in action
bullets: Direct address: 'You know the feeling.'
Rhetorical question: 'How many hours have you already lost today?'
Triple: 'tired, distracted and disconnected'
Anecdote: a quiet family meal, every phone face-down
teach.note: Ask pupils to rewrite each example for a different audience, such as a parent group. Notice how direct address changes (e.g., 'As parents, you will recognise...').

teach.heading: Facts and statistics
bullets: Use plausible, general figures, not made-up precision
Safe: 'many teenagers' or 'more than half'
Avoid invented named studies
Link each figure to your argument
teach.note: Explain that in an exam invented statistics are acceptable if plausible, but exact false quotes can sound weak. Tell pupils to prefer reasonable approximations such as 'nearly half of my class' and always explain their significance.

teach.heading: Tone and restraint
bullets: Passion needs control
One or two devices per paragraph is enough
Avoid exclamation marks except for deliberate effect
Cut anything that sounds like a lecture
teach.note: Show an over-the-top paragraph packed with every device and ask pupils to edit it. A calm, confident voice persuades more than shouting. Link to adab: speaking with respect even when we disagree.

teach.heading: Write a persuasive paragraph
bullets: Point: screens damage sleep
Evidence: a believable anecdote or statistic
Device: a triple or rhetorical question
Link: back to the main argument
teach.note: Model a paragraph for the screens article: 'We have all done it: one more video, one more message, one more scroll. Yet nearly half of my class admit they sleep with their phone beside the pillow, and wake up exhausted. Is a screen really worth your sleep?' Annotate the devices.

practice: Write one rhetorical question, one triple and one example of direct address for the topic 'litter in our community'.
Choose the best device for each aim: (a) shock the reader, (b) make the audience feel included, (c) prove a point.
independent: Write a 100-word persuasive paragraph for the school magazine on 'Young people should have a say in what is taught' using at least three different devices.
Annotate your devices and explain in one sentence why you chose each.
Edit one device out if your paragraph feels overloaded, and justify your edit.
exit: Name two rhetorical devices and one effect for each.
Why can too many techniques weaken an argument?
lessons.homework: Write a short persuasive speech opening (about 120 words) for a school assembly on kindness, using direct address, a triple and an anecdote.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a device card with examples and sentence starters. Stretch: write the same paragraph in two registers and compare their effects.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Paper 2 Section B - Viewpoint writing (Q5)
lessons.title: Question 5: structuring a convincing argument
objectives: Plan a coherent argument with clear paragraphs
Use discourse markers to guide the reader
Include a counter-argument and a strong conclusion

keywords.def: a word or phrase that signposts the argument's direction
an opposing view that you acknowledge and answer
admitting a fair point before arguing against it
an ending that urges the reader to do something

starter: Name three persuasive devices.
Write a hook sentence for an article on sleep.
Give two discourse markers that add a point.

teach.heading: A reliable argument shape
bullets: Opening: hook plus clear stance
Three developed points, strongest last
One counter-argument with a rebuttal
Conclusion: sum up and call to action
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Show a plan on screen for the screens article. Explain why the strongest point goes last: the final point is what the reader remembers. Keep each paragraph focused on one idea.

teach.heading: Paragraph pattern: PEEL-C
bullets: Point: state the idea clearly
Evidence: example, anecdote or statistic
Explain: show why it matters
Link: back to the viewpoint, with a connective
teach.note: Pupils may know PEEL; note the added link to the question. Model with a paragraph on concentration. Ask pupils to underline the link.

teach.heading: Signposting with discourse markers
bullets: Adding: furthermore, in addition, moreover
Contrasting: however, nevertheless, on the other hand
Concluding: ultimately, above all, in short
Do not overuse; vary and place purposefully
teach.note: Ask pupils to find a poor use: 'Firstly... secondly... thirdly...' repeated mechanically. Encourage more natural signposting, such as 'What is more' or 'Consider this'.

teach.heading: Handling the counter-argument
bullets: Acknowledge: 'Some argue that screens help learning.'
Concede: 'There is truth in this...'
Rebut: 'But learning needs focus, not constant alerts.'
Stay respectful of other views
teach.note: Connect to adab in disagreement: representing the other side fairly. Model one rebuttal. Remind pupils that the counter-argument strengthens their credibility.

teach.heading: Endings that stick
bullets: Return to your hook or anecdote
End with a challenge or call to action
Use a short, memorable final sentence
Do not introduce brand new arguments
teach.note: Give examples of weak endings ('In conclusion, I have said what I think') and strong ones ('Tonight, put the phone face-down and see what you hear.').

practice: Put these paragraph topics in the best order for the screens article: counter-argument, sleep, hook, call to action, concentration, friendship.
Write a counter-argument sentence and a rebuttal sentence for the claim 'Screens help students learn'.
independent: Plan and write (30 minutes) a speech for your school assembly: ''Schools should make more time for kindness.' Write a speech to persuade your school.' Use a hook, three points, one counter-argument and a call to action.
Highlight your discourse markers.
Underline your strongest sentence and your weakest, and rewrite the weakest.
exit: Name the four parts of a convincing argument.
Give one discourse marker for contrast.
lessons.homework: Finish your speech to a polished draft, aiming for 450-500 words, with a memorable final sentence.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a paragraph frame, a discourse marker bank and a pre-filled plan. Stretch: weave in a short quotation or proverb that supports your stance and is clearly sourced or general.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Paper 2 Section B - Viewpoint writing (Q5)
lessons.title: Technical accuracy and polishing for Question 5
objectives: Spot and correct common technical errors
Use punctuation and sentence variety for persuasive effect
Proofread a full piece systematically

keywords.def: the verb matches its subject in number
an unintended switch between past and present
words that sound alike but differ in meaning or spelling
marking where sentences begin and end

starter: Correct the comma splice: 'Homework matters, many pupils ignore it.'
Choose: there / their / they're. '___ going to lose ___ sleep over it.'
What is a call to action?

teach.heading: The 16 marks
bullets: Sentence demarcation and punctuation
Spelling, from simple to ambitious words
Grammar, including agreement and tense
Vocabulary chosen for precision and effect
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Remind pupils that technical accuracy is 40 percent of the Q5 marks. A well-structured argument with frequent errors can lose many marks.

teach.heading: The big five errors
bullets: Comma splices and run-on sentences
Apostrophes: its / it's, pupils / pupil's
Homophones: their, there, your, you're
Subject-verb agreement: 'the teachers was' is wrong
Informal slips: 'a lot', 'could of', 'gonna'
teach.note: Take each error and give a fast fix. 'Could of' is a mishearing of 'could have'. 'Alot' is two words: 'a lot' (and in formal writing, prefer 'many' or 'much'). Use quick-fire corrections.

teach.heading: Punctuation for persuasion
bullets: Question marks for rhetorical questions
Dash for emphasis: 'Screens steal time - and sleep.'
Colon for a reveal: 'The truth is simple: we are tired.'
Exclamation marks: use sparingly
teach.note: Show that punctuation can create rhythm for speeches and articles. Warn pupils against sentences that end with several exclamation marks.

teach.heading: Proofread in layers
bullets: Pass 1: sentences, capitals and full stops
Pass 2: apostrophes and commas
Pass 3: spelling and homophones
Pass 4: read aloud in your head for flow
teach.note: Teach pupils to proofread in several short passes rather than one vague one. Do a live demonstration with an error-filled paragraph.

teach.heading: Upgrade vocabulary safely
bullets: Replace weak words: bad, good, thing, big
Choose precise words: damaging, beneficial, element, significant
Check you know spelling and meaning
Keep to a clear, controlled formal register
teach.note: Give a short list for pupils to apply: 'bad for you' to 'detrimental to wellbeing'. Warn against swapping in long words incorrectly; accuracy counts more than size.

practice: Correct this sentence: 'Its important that students gets enough sleep, alot of them dont.'
Add punctuation: 'Many teenagers stay up late scrolling the result is tiredness poor focus and bad moods.'
independent: Proofread and correct (at least ten errors): 'Their are many reason why young people should have a voice, its not fair that adults decide everything. In my school the teachers was never asked, we was just told. I seen how this effects pupils, alot of them feel ignored. Its time we was listened too.'
Rewrite the corrected paragraph so it is more formal and persuasive.
List the three errors you most often make and write a rule for each.
exit: Correct: 'Your going to loose your phone if you dont put it away.'
Name one way to proofread in layers.
lessons.homework: Proofread your speech from Lesson 10 using the layered method and list ten corrections you made.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide an error-hunt checklist with colour codes and a bank of correct forms. Stretch: write a short paragraph that deliberately uses a colon, a dash and a semi-colon, and explain why each is correct.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Paper 2 Section B - Viewpoint writing (Q5)
lessons.title: Timed Question 5 and whole-paper exam technique
objectives: Plan and write a timed viewpoint piece
Allocate time sensibly across the whole of Paper 2
Set targets from self-assessment

keywords.def: planning how long to spend on each part of an exam
a checklist of what a strong answer includes
a specific action to improve your next response
answering an opposing argument

starter: Name one method for proofreading a piece of writing.
Give a discourse marker for contrast and one for addition.
What are the five questions on Paper 2 and their marks?

teach.heading: Whole-paper timing
bullets: Paper 2 is 1 hour 45 minutes in total
About an hour for Section A, including reading
About 45 minutes for Section B
Q4 and Q5 deserve the most time
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Walk through a suggested timeline: 15 min reading, Q1 about 5, Q2 about 10, Q3 about 15, Q4 about 20; then Q5 planning and writing in the remaining time. Tell pupils to practise it under timed conditions before the real exam.

teach.heading: Today's task
bullets: Choose one: 'Homework should be banned.' (article)
Or: 'Young people should vote at sixteen.' (speech)
5 minutes plan, 30 minutes write, 5 minutes proofread
Aim for about 450 words
teach.note: Choice is allowed for practice, though in the exam there is one task. Remind pupils that adab in debate means arguing a position without insulting people who hold another. Offer a short model plan for the voting task.

teach.heading: Success criteria
bullets: Clear audience, purpose and form
Developed argument with a counter-argument
Rhetorical devices used purposefully
Accurate, varied punctuation and spelling
teach.note: Pupils tick off criteria after writing. Ask them to choose one criterion to prioritise while writing.

teach.heading: Self-assessment
bullets: Highlight your best paragraph green
Underline any errors you spot, then fix them
Write two targets for your next Q5
Be specific and measurable
teach.note: Model one target: 'Include a rebuttal in every counter-argument.' Collect targets in the chat. This feeds into your next feedback cycle.

practice: Spend 5 minutes writing a plan: stance, three points, one counter-argument, ending.
Write your opening two sentences and check they show the right register for the audience.
independent: Write your timed Q5 piece (30 minutes), then proofread for 5 minutes.
Complete the success criteria checklist and highlight your strongest paragraph.
Write two specific targets for next time.
exit: State one target for your next Q5 response.
How long should you spend planning Q5?
lessons.homework: Redraft your weakest paragraph from today's timed piece, applying one target, and submit both versions.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: allow a scaffolded plan and sentence starters; extra time as needed. Stretch: add a powerful closing paragraph that returns to the opening image or question.

lessons.unit: P2-A-Q1: Paper 2 Section A: Question 1, true statements
lessons.title: Question 1: choosing the four true statements
lessons.bigQuestion: How do I judge a statement is true when it sounds almost right?
objectives: Read a Paper 2 Question 1 and find evidence for each statement in the named lines
Tell the difference between true, false and 'sounds true' statements
Complete the question quickly and accurately
successCriteria: All: select statements supported by the text
Most: reject statements with one small error
Some: justify each choice by line number in under four minutes
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: reading survey data (one in five, nearly half)
lessons.smsc: Moral: truthfulness and care with evidence (sidq)

keywords.def: stated directly
suggested, not stated
a statement fully supported by the text
a statement that looks possible but contains an error
an area sheltered from sunlight

starter: Bismillah. Retrieval: what is Paper 2 Question 1 worth and what does it test?
Fractions: what does 'one in five' mean as a fraction and a percentage?
What is the difference between 'a mile' and 'a kilometre'?

teach.heading: Source A

quote.text:
1 Every weekday at 8.15, my street turns into a car park. Engines idle, horns
2 blare, and a small boy is lifted from a 4x4 and set down like a parcel, twenty
3 metres from the school gate. The school is just a mile from our house, but
4 hardly anyone walks it any more. Last year a survey in our town found that
5 only one child in five walked to school; nearly half arrived by car.
6 I understand why. The roads are busier, parents are rushed, and nobody
7 wants to be late for work. Yet I have started walking my daughter, Mina, the
8 whole mile. It takes twenty-five minutes. She complains for the first five,
9 then she begins to notice things: the baker's van, a heron on the canal,
10 the way frost lingers in the shade. By the gate she is calmer and
11 chatting. I am convinced that those twenty-five minutes teach her more
12 than any worksheet.
quote.source: Source A: original 21st-century newspaper column written for TGA

teach.note: Read aloud. Pupils number the lines. All sources in this unit are original and written for TGA. Cultural context: the school run is a British phrase for the morning trip to school; a 4x4 is a large car; 'frost' is ice crystals on cold mornings. Cultural context for both sources: Source A is a modern British newspaper column about the school run (parents driving children to school; a 4x4 is a large car). Source B imitates a Victorian letter: the 1870 Elementary Education Act brought schools to many poor villages. A turnpike was a toll road, a pinafore a child's apron-like overall, a mistress a female teacher, and a carrier's cart a horse-drawn delivery cart.

teach.heading: The Question 1 routine
cycle: Underline the key word or number in each statement
Find the matching line in the stated lines
Tick only if every part is supported
Stop at four; check numbers and quantifiers
teach.note: Say: four marks, four statements; if more than four are chosen, only the first four are marked, so do not over-choose. Teach pupils to underline the key detail in each statement and match it to a line. Ask which words hide errors: 'all', 'never', 'always', 'only', numbers.

teach.heading: Worked model

model.problem: Read lines 1 to 8. Choose four statements that are true. A: The school is two miles away. B: A boy is lifted from a large car. C: Nearly half of children arrive by car. D: Hardly anyone walks to school. E: Mina walks in five minutes. F: Parents are rushed.
steps: A: line 3 says 'just a mile', so A is false.
B: lines 1-2 say a small boy is lifted from a 4x4, so B is true.
C: line 5 says nearly half arrived by car, so C is true.
D: line 4 says 'hardly anyone walks', so D is true; E: line 8 says twenty-five minutes, so E is false; F: line 6 says 'parents are rushed', so F is true.
model.answer: True: B, C, D and F. (A and E are false.)

teach.note: Walk through each statement. Point out trap A has a changed number and C has a reversed fact. Link the idea of explicit to AO1: the evidence is in the text.

teach.heading: Hinge question

check.q: Which statement is true according to lines 4 to 8?
options: One child in four walks to school.
Mina walks to school without complaining.
check.why: C matches line 8. A changes the number in line 5; B ignores 'She complains for the first five'.

teach.note: Mini-whiteboards. The answer is C. A changes 'one in five' to 'one in four'; B contradicts line 8.

teach.heading: Common error

misconception.wrong: 'Hardly anyone walks' is the same as 'nobody walks', so it is false.
misconception.right: 'Hardly anyone' means very few, which matches line 4; read each statement against the exact words.

teach.note: Ask pupils to read the statement twice. Say that one wrong word makes the whole statement false. Idiom: 'the devil is in the detail'.

practice: Using lines 6 to 12, write two true statements and two false statements for a partner.
Mark a partner's statements and write the line number for each answer.
Decide: 'Mina notices a heron on the canal.' True or false? Give the line.
independent: Core: Complete an original Question 1: lines 6 to 12, eight statements, choose four true.
Extend: Write your own eight statements for lines 1 to 5 with a tick list.
Stretch: Rewrite three false statements as true ones and explain the changes.
exit: How many statements should you choose?
Why must you check numbers and 'only' or 'all'?
Big question: how do I decide a statement is true?
lessons.homework: Write eight statements (four true, four false) for a news report you find and swap with a family member.
lessons.send: SEND: enlarge the text, add line numbers and allow a ruler to track lines; give a tick-box table with the line number column. EAL/international: pre-teach 'idle', 'blare', 'lingers', 'canal'; idiom 'the school run' and 'the devil is in the detail'; stems: 'Line 4 says that ...', 'This is false because ...'. Cultural context for both sources: Source A is a modern British newspaper column about the school run (parents driving children to school; a 4x4 is a large car). Source B imitates a Victorian letter: the 1870 Elementary Education Act brought schools to many poor villages. A turnpike was a toll road, a pinafore a child's apron-like overall, a mistress a female teacher, and a carrier's cart a horse-drawn delivery cart. Stretch: write a statement that is true but implicit, not explicit.

lessons.unit: P2-A-Q2: Paper 2 Section A: Question 2, summary
lessons.title: Question 2: a model summary of differences across two sources
lessons.bigQuestion: How do I merge two texts into one clear answer without listing quotations?
objectives: Select the differences that answer the specific focus of the question
Infer meaning rather than copy details
Write in continuous prose using comparative language
successCriteria: All: write two differences with evidence
Most: use comparative connectives and infer meaning
Some: synthesise both sources in a single, concise paragraph
lessons.crossCurricular: History: the 1870 Education Act and daily life
lessons.smsc: Social: understanding how childhood has changed

keywords.def: give the main points concisely
combine ideas from both sources
work out meaning from clues
a connective showing contrast
what the question asks you to concentrate on

starter: Bismillah. Retrieval: how many marks is Paper 2 Question 2 and what is its AO?
Write a sentence using 'whereas' to contrast a cat and a dog.
Name two differences between a letter and a newspaper column.

teach.heading: Both sources

quote.text:
1 Thornbury, 14th October 1871
2 My dear Sister,
3 You ask how the children fare at the new school, and I am glad to say they thrive,
4 though I confess the road to it is no light matter. Every morning, whatever the weather,
5 Thomas and little Ellen must walk the full three miles by the old turnpike, with their
6 dinner in a tin and their boots, I fear, scarcely sound. In November the lane is a
7 river of mud, and last week Ellen arrived with her stockings quite sodden, and was
8 scolded by the mistress for the state of her pinafore. Yet I would not keep them at home.
9 Education is the only fortune a poor man's child may hope to inherit, and I shall not
10 see it wasted for want of a little weariness in the legs. Thomas says the walk is the best
11 part of the day, for he and the Pritchard boys race the carrier's cart, and he knows where
12 every bird builds its nest.
13 Pray give my love to Papa, and believe me, your affectionate sister, Eliza
quote.source: Source B: original letter in the style of 1871, written for TGA (pastiche, not a real historical document)

teach.note: Reprint Source A (lines 1-12) and Source B (lines 1-13) for pupils. Say this lesson uses both. Source B has unfamiliar details; 'turnpike' (toll road), 'pinafore' (child's overall), 'mistress' (teacher), 'sodden' (soaking wet). Cultural context for both sources: Source A is a modern British newspaper column about the school run (parents driving children to school; a 4x4 is a large car). Source B imitates a Victorian letter: the 1870 Elementary Education Act brought schools to many poor villages. A turnpike was a toll road, a pinafore a child's apron-like overall, a mistress a female teacher, and a carrier's cart a horse-drawn delivery cart.

teach.heading: The focus and the plan
teach.note: Give the question and ask pupils to colour-code differences in two colours. Note that the question asks only for differences in how children travel to school, so facts about the parents' feelings are not needed. Pupils should refer to both sources in every sentence, not write two paragraphs about two texts.

teach.heading: Worked model: an eight-mark summary

model.problem: Write a summary of the differences between the way children travel to school in Source A and Source B. (8 marks)
steps: State the focus: the way children get to school.
Pair the evidence: one mile versus three miles; car versus foot.
Infer: Source A implies walking is now a choice; Source B implies it is a necessity.
Use comparative connectives: whereas, in contrast, while.
Close with a synthesised point.
model.answer: In Source A most children are driven the short mile to school, whereas the children in Source B have no choice but to walk three miles in all weathers. The modern parent chooses to walk, which suggests walking is now a deliberate habit, while in 1871 it is an unavoidable hardship, shown by the 'river of mud' and unsound boots. In contrast to the calm, observant Mina, Thomas turns the journey into a race with the carrier's cart. The sources therefore show a shift from necessity to choice.

teach.note: Model aloud; underline the comparative words and the inferences (in italics). Note that the paragraph never copies more than two words in a row. Time guide: about ten minutes.

teach.heading: Hinge question

check.q: Which is the best opening sentence?
options: 'Source A says the street is a car park and Source B says it is a river of mud.'
'In Source A most children are driven a short distance, whereas in Source B they must walk three miles.'
check.why: B answers the focus and compares in one sentence. A lists quotations; C is off focus.

teach.note: Mini-whiteboards. The answer is B. A is a list of quotations; C is about attitudes, not the focus.

teach.heading: Inference ladder
bullets: Detail: boots, I fear, scarcely sound.
Inference: the family cannot afford good boots.
Link: in Source A, parents choose cars.
Difference: poverty then, convenience now.
teach.note: Show how a detail becomes inference: 'boots scarcely sound' leads to 'the family are poor and cannot afford proper boots'.

practice: Write a sentence of difference about time using 'whereas'.
Infer one thing from 'dinner in a tin' and compare with Source A.
Colour-code a partner's sentence for evidence and inference.
independent: Core: Write a six-sentence summary of the differences in travel to school.
Extend: Write a summary of differences in the conditions the children face, with inference.
Stretch: Write a 150-word summary that also synthesises the changes over time.
exit: Name two comparative connectives.
Why is a list of quotations not a summary?
Big question: how do I merge two texts into one answer?
lessons.homework: Write a 100-word summary of the differences between a school day now and 100 years ago, using whichever sources you can find (a family member, a library book).
lessons.send: SEND: give a comparison table and sentence starters; limit to four sentences. EAL/international: pre-teach 'turnpike', 'pinafore', 'mistress', 'sodden', 'unavoidable'; idiom 'to come down to' = to depend; stems: 'In Source A ..., whereas in Source B ...', 'This suggests that ...'. Cultural context for both sources: Source A is a modern British newspaper column about the school run (parents driving children to school; a 4x4 is a large car). Source B imitates a Victorian letter: the 1870 Elementary Education Act brought schools to many poor villages. A turnpike was a toll road, a pinafore a child's apron-like overall, a mistress a female teacher, and a carrier's cart a horse-drawn delivery cart. Stretch: include a counter-point where the sources are similar.

lessons.unit: P2-A-Q3: Paper 2 Section A: Question 3, language
lessons.title: Question 3: language in a 19th-century letter
lessons.bigQuestion: How does a writer's choice of words reveal her feelings and persuade us?
objectives: Decode 19th-century vocabulary and sentence structures
Analyse tone, understatement and metaphor for effect
Write a Level 4 paragraph on a non-fiction source
successCriteria: All: quote and explain a word's effect
Most: analyse tone and method with terminology
Some: link language to the writer's purpose and attitude in a sustained paragraph
lessons.smsc: Moral: sacrifice and aspiration (a parent's hope for children)

keywords.def: the attitude or mood of the writing
saying less than the truth to emphasise it
understatement using a negative, such as 'no light matter'
level of formality
deliberate exaggeration

starter: Bismillah. Retrieval: name two differences between Source A and Source B (last lesson).
Define 'tone' using two adjectives.
What is the effect of a metaphor?
