Source B imitates a Victorian letter: the 1870 Elementary Education Act brought schools to many poor villages. A turnpike was a toll road, a pinafore a child's apron-like overall, a mistress a female teacher, and a carrier's cart a horse-drawn delivery cart.

teach.heading: Method: tone, technique, effect
cycle: Explain the effect on the reader
Link to the writer's purpose and attitude
teach.note: Remind pupils that Question 3 (12 marks) is on one source only and the same Q-M-E-Z routine applies. In Paper 2 attitude and purpose matter; so every comment links to the writer's point of view. Ask pupils to find three words where the tone shifts from worry to resolve.

teach.heading: Worked model: a Level 4 paragraph

model.problem: How does the writer use language to show her attitude to the children's walk to school? (12 marks)
steps: Tone: the formal 'I confess' creates a dutiful, honest tone.
Litotes: 'no light matter' understates the difficulty, so the hardship feels gently stated, not exaggerated.
Metaphor: 'a river of mud' vividly shows the dangers of the lane.
Metaphor: 'the only fortune a poor man's child may hope to inherit' turns education into wealth.
Zoom: 'weariness' is small and manageable, so she dismisses the hardship.
model.answer: The writer adopts a formal, dutiful tone from the outset: 'I confess' suggests honest admission, as though she is reluctant to burden her sister with complaints. The litotes 'no light matter' understates the difficulty, so the reader senses a hardship stoically accepted. The metaphor 'a river of mud' is vivid and slightly comic, but it also emphasises how dangerous the lane is for a small child. Yet she refuses to keep the children at home, calling education 'the only fortune a poor man's child may hope to inherit'. The metaphor of wealth shows that, for this family, learning is the only route to security, so the mother's pride outweighs her worry. The understated 'a little weariness in the legs' dismisses the hardship, which implies a stern determination that the reader admires.

teach.note: Read twice and ask for the zoomed words ('confess', 'inherit'). Point out that this paragraph deals with two features and the shift, and about 150 words is realistic. Mention that 'no light matter' is litotes (understatement using a negative).

teach.heading: Hinge question

check.q: What is the effect of 'a little weariness in the legs'?
options: It understates the hardship, showing the mother's determination.
It states that the children are strong.
It is an example of onomatopoeia.
check.why: A explains the understatement and its effect on tone. B is not supported; C is incorrect (no sound).

teach.note: Mini-whiteboards. The answer is A. B ignores the effect; C names a feature not in the text.

teach.heading: Terminology bank
bullets: tone: dutiful, stoical, affectionate, firm
method: litotes, metaphor, hyperbole, direct address
effect: reassures, persuades, evokes sympathy
link: purpose and attitude
teach.note: Stress that terminology supports analysis; it does not replace it. Offer EAL pupils the sentence frames.

practice: Analyse 'whatever the weather' in one Q-M-E-Z sentence.
What is the effect of 'dinner in a tin'?
Identify one formal word and explain why it fits the period.
independent: Core: Write a four-sentence paragraph on the metaphor 'a river of mud'.
Extend: Write a full paragraph (150 words) on tone and understatement.
Stretch: Write a two-paragraph answer analysing how the tone changes from worry to resolve.
exit: Name two methods in Source B.
Why is 'no light matter' called understatement?
Big question: how does a writer's language reveal her feelings?
lessons.homework: Write a 100-word letter in the style of Source B about a modern problem and list three formal features you used.
lessons.send: SEND: provide a three-column analysis grid (quote, method, effect) and a tone word bank. EAL/international: pre-teach 'dutiful', 'stoical', 'understatement', 'sodden', 'confess'; idiom 'to put a brave face on it' = to hide worry; stems: 'The tone is ... because ...', 'The writer implies ...'. Cultural context for both sources: Source A is a modern British newspaper column about the school run (parents driving children to school; a 4x4 is a large car). Source B imitates a Victorian letter: the 1870 Elementary Education Act brought schools to many poor villages. A turnpike was a toll road, a pinafore a child's apron-like overall, a mistress a female teacher, and a carrier's cart a horse-drawn delivery cart. Stretch: compare the tone with a modern parent's tone in Source A.

lessons.unit: P2-A-Q4: Paper 2 Section A: Question 4, comparison of perspectives
lessons.title: Question 4: writing a comparison of perspectives and methods
lessons.bigQuestion: How do two writers' different worlds shape how they write about the same thing?
objectives: Compare two writers' perspectives with references to both
Compare methods: language and structure
Use comparative connectives to link ideas
successCriteria: All: write about both sources with evidence
Most: compare perspectives and methods using connectives
Some: write a sustained, perceptive comparison tracing perspective, language and structure across both texts
lessons.crossCurricular: History: social change from 1871 to today
lessons.smsc: Social and cultural: empathy across time and place

keywords.def: the position or attitude from which something is seen
a link word showing similarity or difference
the language and structure choices a writer makes
a writer's opinion
a feeling about a topic

starter: Bismillah. Retrieval: write one difference between the two sources about distance.
Name two comparative connectives for similarity and two for difference.
What does AO3 ask for?

teach.heading: The question

quote.text: Compare how the two writers convey their different perspectives and feelings about children walking to school. In your answer, you could: compare their different perspectives and feelings; compare the methods they use to convey their perspectives; support your response with references to both texts. (16 marks)

teach.note: Display the question with both sources available. Ask pupils to underline the key words 'perspectives' and 'methods'. Stress that Q4 is worth 16 marks and uses the whole of both sources. Pupils plan for three minutes then write for about fifteen.

teach.heading: A comparison grid

head: Feature
Source A (column)
Source B (letter)
rows: walking is a hardship worth bearing
report, then resolve, then a joyful detail

teach.note: Fill the grid with pupils. Ask: who is the audience and how does it change the writing? Draw out that Source A is a published column seeking to persuade, Source B a private letter reporting and reassuring. Ask pupils to find a similarity too (both value learning).

teach.heading: Worked model: two comparative paragraphs

model.problem: Compare how the two writers convey their different perspectives and feelings about children walking to school. (16 marks)
steps: Link perspective and method in each paragraph.
Use quotation from both sources every time.
Use connectives: whereas, similarly, in contrast.
Comment on structure as well as language.
Finish with a short overview.
model.answer: Both writers value what children gain on the journey, but they convey this very differently. The modern columnist, who chooses to walk, presents the journey as a gift: the simile of a boy 'set down like a parcel' mocks the car parent, while the calm Mina who notices 'a heron on the canal' shows what is gained. In contrast, the Victorian mother treats the walk as a necessary hardship, conveyed by the metaphor 'a river of mud' and the understatement 'no light matter'. Whereas the column moves from a problem to a personal solution to persuade the public, the letter moves from worry to determination to reassure a sister, ending with the joyful detail of the boys racing the cart. Both therefore see the walk as valuable, but for the columnist it is an escape from modern life, and for Eliza an unavoidable price of education.

teach.note: Read aloud and underline the connectives. Point out every sentence refers to both sources, with quotation and method. Ask where perspective and method are linked.

teach.heading: Hinge question

check.q: Which sentence best compares?
options: Source A is about cars. Source B is about mud.
Whereas the columnist chooses to walk, Eliza accepts the walk as unavoidable, shown by 'no light matter'.
check.why: C compares perspectives with a connective and evidence. A is separate; B has no evidence.

teach.note: Mini-whiteboards. The answer is C. A treats the sources separately; B is a similarity without evidence.

teach.heading: Structure comments
bullets: Source A: starts with a problem, ends with a conclusion.
Source B: starts with greeting, ends with warmth.
Both end on a positive image.
Compare: public persuasion versus private reassurance.
teach.note: Remind pupils that Q4 rewards methods, and that structure counts. Ask them to find the shifts.

practice: Write one sentence comparing the tone of the two sources with a connective.
Compare one language method in each source.
Write a sentence comparing the endings.
independent: Core: Write one comparative paragraph on perspective, with quotations from both sources.
Extend: Write two paragraphs: one on perspective, one on methods (language and structure).
Stretch: Write a full 300-word answer with an overview and a perceptive conclusion.
exit: Name three comparative connectives.
Why must every paragraph refer to both sources?
Big question: how do different worlds shape how writers write?
lessons.homework: Write 120 words comparing a modern and an old text of your choice (a family letter and a text message) using three connectives.
lessons.send: SEND: give a pre-filled comparison grid, a connectives bank and a two-paragraph frame. EAL/international: pre-teach 'perspective', 'whereas', 'unavoidable', 'necessity'; idiom 'on the one hand ... on the other hand'; stems: 'Both writers ..., but ...', 'Whereas Source A ..., Source B ...'. Cultural context for both sources: Source A is a modern British newspaper column about the school run (parents driving children to school; a 4x4 is a large car). Source B imitates a Victorian letter: the 1870 Elementary Education Act brought schools to many poor villages. A turnpike was a toll road, a pinafore a child's apron-like overall, a mistress a female teacher, and a carrier's cart a horse-drawn delivery cart. Stretch: add a counter-reading in which the columnist is less sincere.

lessons.unit: P2-A-Q4: Paper 2 Section A: Question 4, comparison of perspectives
lessons.title: Question 4: embedding evidence and weaving methods into comparison
lessons.bigQuestion: How can I make every sentence of a comparison do two jobs at once?
objectives: Embed short quotations within comparative sentences
Combine perspective, method and effect in one sentence
Revise a draft comparison for balance and precision
successCriteria: All: use quotations from both sources in one answer
Most: link a method to a perspective in each sentence
Some: write tightly integrated comparative sentences with perceptive inference
lessons.smsc: Social: listening fairly to different generations

keywords.def: fit a short quotation into your own sentence
combine two ideas in one sentence
equal attention to both sources
a meaning worked out from clues
a short summing-up of the main comparison

starter: Bismillah. Retrieval: name the three things a Q4 answer compares.
Embed the quotation 'a river of mud' in your own sentence.
Which source is more formal and why?

teach.heading: From a weak to a strong sentence

left.title: Weak (one job)
points: Source A says the street is a car park.
Source B says the road is hard.

right.title: Strong (many jobs)
points: The columnist mocks the car parent with the simile 'like a parcel', whereas Eliza accepts hardship with the understated 'no light matter'.

teach.note: Show the progression. Ask pupils to count the jobs each sentence does (perspective, quotation, method, comparison). Note that weak sentences do one job. Both source texts reprinted in the pack.

teach.heading: Balance check
bullets: Count quotations: A and B equal?
Do both sources appear in each paragraph?
Is there one structure comment each?
Is there one inference about each writer?
teach.note: Say that a lopsided answer (four paragraphs on A, one on B) limits marks. Ask pupils to count references. Stress using short quotations.

teach.heading: Worked model: improving a draft

model.problem: Improve this draft: 'Source A is modern. Source B is old. Source A walks. Source B also walks.'
steps: Replace listing with a comparative sentence.
Add a quotation from each source.
Name a method and its effect for each.
Add an inference about the writer's perspective.
model.answer: Whereas the columnist walks by choice, presenting it as calming through the gentle detail of 'a heron on the canal', Eliza's children walk of necessity, with 'dinner in a tin' implying a family with little money; the contrast shows how walking has changed from hardship to luxury.

teach.note: Look at the revision steps. Ask pupils to read the draft and the revised version aloud and identify what changed. Note that the revision changes 'also' to 'whereas', adds a method and an inference.

teach.heading: Hinge question

check.q: Which sentence is best balanced?
options: The columnist uses a simile 'like a parcel' and a list of calm details and a conclusion.
The columnist mocks car drivers with 'like a parcel', whereas Eliza dignifies hardship with 'no light matter'.
Both writers are good at writing.
check.why: B uses evidence from both sources and compares attitude and method. A is about one source; C has no evidence.

teach.note: Mini-whiteboards. The answer is B. A is not balanced; C does not use evidence.

teach.heading: Overview sentence
bullets: Overall, both see value in the journey.
Yet one sees choice, the other necessity.
Methods differ: persuasion versus reassurance.
Write it in 25 words or fewer.
teach.note: End with a single, clear sentence of overview. EAL stem 'Overall, ...'.

practice: Combine two weak sentences into one comparative sentence with quotations.
Write an overview sentence for the two sources.
Count and balance the quotations in a partner's paragraph.
independent: Core: Rewrite a weak comparison paragraph so every sentence has a quotation from each source.
Extend: Write a full paragraph comparing structure, with an inference.
Stretch: Write a timed 250-word answer and self-mark against balance and precision.
exit: What is a quotation that is 'embedded'?
Why must a comparison be balanced?
Big question: how can a sentence do two jobs at once?
lessons.homework: Take your earlier Q4 answer, count quotations from each source, and rewrite one paragraph to make it balanced.
lessons.send: SEND: provide a four-box sentence builder (quotation A, quotation B, connective, effect). EAL/international: pre-teach 'embed', 'integrate', 'balance', 'overview'; idiom 'to kill two birds with one stone'; stems: 'Whereas ..., ...', 'Overall, ...'. Cultural context for both sources: Source A is a modern British newspaper column about the school run (parents driving children to school; a 4x4 is a large car). Source B imitates a Victorian letter: the 1870 Elementary Education Act brought schools to many poor villages. A turnpike was a toll road, a pinafore a child's apron-like overall, a mistress a female teacher, and a carrier's cart a horse-drawn delivery cart. Stretch: compare how each writer addresses the reader (direct address in A, intimate address in B).

lessons.unit: P2-B-Q5: Paper 2 Section B: Question 5, viewpoint writing
lessons.title: Question 5: audience, purpose and form (a modelled article)
lessons.bigQuestion: How do I make my own view sound convincing and suited to the reader?
objectives: Read a Question 5 prompt and identify audience, purpose and form
Plan an article with a clear line of argument
Write a controlled, persuasive opening paragraph
successCriteria: All: state the audience, purpose and form
Most: write an article with a headline, an opening, paragraphs and a conclusion
Some: control register and structure so the article is shaped for its readers
lessons.smsc: Spiritual and social: humility and care for others in how we walk through the world

keywords.def: the people the writing is for
what the writing is meant to do
the type of text, such as article, speech or letter
the level of formality
the title of a newspaper article

starter: Bismillah. Retrieval: how many marks are there for content and organisation and how many for technical accuracy?
Name three features of a newspaper article.
What is the difference between audience and purpose?

teach.heading: The task

quote.text: 'Children today should walk or cycle to school instead of being driven.' Write an article for your school magazine in which you explain your point of view on this statement. (40 marks)

teach.note: Display the task. Ask pupils to underline audience (readers of the school magazine), purpose (persuade) and form (article). The task links to the Section A sources but the pupil states their own view. A short note: many pupils will have a personal story about walking or travelling to school; welcome these. Qur'an 25:63 describes the servants of the Most Merciful as those who walk on the earth with humility; a teacher may mention it as a reflection, not as part of the exam.

teach.heading: Compare forms
teach.note: Highlight that all three forms persuade but with different features. Ask pupils which is easiest to control and why. For EAL pupils: 'Dear Editor' and 'Yours faithfully' are conventions of formal letters.

teach.heading: Worked model: plan and opening

model.problem: Plan and open the article on 'Children should walk or cycle to school'.
steps: Headline: a punchy pun or question.
Opening: a short personal anecdote or striking image.
State your view clearly.
Plan three paragraphs: health, independence, community; one counter-argument; a call to action.
model.answer: HEADLINE: Time to Take the Long Way. Every morning on Elm Road, the traffic crawls and the pavements are empty. Yet the quickest journey is not always the best one. As someone who walks twenty minutes to school each day, I believe that every child who can should walk or cycle, because the journey makes us healthier, more independent and better neighbours.

teach.note: Read the plan and the opening paragraph. Ask pupils to annotate: headline, anecdote, direct address, claim, sign-posting. Point out that the opening is under 90 words and sets out the line of argument.

teach.heading: Hinge question

check.q: Which opening best suits a persuasive school-magazine article?
options: Every morning on Elm Road, the traffic crawls and the pavements are empty. Yet the quickest journey is not always the best one.
Once upon a time there was a boy who went to school.
The school has 800 pupils and 12 buses.
check.why: A has a hook and a view. B is narrative; C informs without a stance.

teach.note: Mini-whiteboards. The answer is A. B is a story, C is a report.

teach.heading: Register and tone
bullets: Use 'I' sparingly and with purpose.
Avoid slang; use contractions rarely.
Address the reader: 'you', 'we', 'our school'.
Keep paragraphs short, linked by connectives.
teach.note: Say: friendly but formal. Idiom: 'to strike the right note'.

practice: Underline audience, purpose and form in a new task: a speech to parents about homework.
Write a headline with a pun for your article.
Write three topic sentences for your plan.
independent: Core: Write the headline and opening paragraph for the article.
Extend: Write the first two body paragraphs and a counter-argument.
Stretch: Write the complete 400-word article in 35 minutes.
exit: State the audience, purpose and form of the model task.
Why is a plan worth five minutes?
Big question: how do I make my view convincing and suited to the reader?
lessons.homework: Write a different opening (a speech version) for the same view, and list the changes from the article version.
lessons.send: SEND: give a planning frame (headline, hook, three reasons, counter-argument, call to action). EAL/international: pre-teach 'strapline', 'headline', 'counter-argument', 'campaign'; idiom 'a hook' (an opening that grabs attention); stems: 'I firmly believe that ...', 'Some people argue that ... however ...'. Cultural note: UK school magazines and local newspapers are common forums for pupil opinion. Stretch: shape the article for a hostile audience of parents who drive.

lessons.unit: P2-B-Q5: Paper 2 Section B: Question 5, viewpoint writing
lessons.title: Question 5: persuasive techniques, structure and polish
lessons.bigQuestion: Which techniques actually persuade, and when do they become too much?
objectives: Use rhetorical techniques accurately and with restraint
Structure a persuasive text with sign-posting and a counter-argument
Proofread for technical accuracy
successCriteria: All: use three persuasive devices correctly
Most: shape paragraphs with sign-posting and a counter-argument
Some: control register, vary sentence length and proofread to achieve a polished piece
lessons.crossCurricular: Speech and Debate; PSHE: healthy choices
lessons.smsc: Moral: honest persuasion, without exaggeration that misleads

keywords.def: a question asked for effect
a list of three
words chosen to arouse feelings
an opposing view that you answer
words that guide the reader through the argument

starter: Bismillah. Retrieval: name three features of an article.
Write a rhetorical question about school uniforms.
Give a triplet about the benefits of exercise.

teach.heading: A FOREST of techniques

head: Letter
Technique
Example
rows: a mile takes about twenty minutes
walking is the best way to wake up
Why sit in traffic when you could stroll?
only one child in five walks

teach.note: Introduce the mnemonic A-F-O-R-E-S-T and say it is a memory aid, not a checklist: techniques must fit the argument. Warn about overuse: too many devices read as forced. Remind that statistics must be plausible and you may invent them, but keep them believable.

teach.heading: Structure with sign-posting
teach.note: Say that persuasion needs order. Move through the order and ask pupils to give a connective for each stage. Idiom: 'to have the last word'.

teach.heading: Worked model: a persuasive body paragraph

model.problem: Write a paragraph arguing that walking to school improves health, including a counter-argument.
steps: Topic sentence with a clear claim.
Evidence: a believable fact or statistic.
Technique: a rhetorical question and a triplet.
Counter-argument: 'Admittedly ...' followed by a reply.
Link back to the thesis.
model.answer: Walking to school makes children healthier. A mile on foot takes only twenty minutes, yet nearly half of pupils spend it slumped in the back seat of a car. Surely a little fresh air is a small price for brighter, steadier and calmer mornings? Admittedly, some families live too far away or are pressed for time; but even walking the last five minutes from a drop-off point can transform the day. A healthy journey is the first lesson of the day.

teach.note: Read the paragraph, then underline devices (question, triplet, emotive word, statistic, counter-argument). Ask pupils whether any device is overdone (no). Point out the register stays formal and the paragraph ends with a link back to the thesis.

teach.heading: Hinge question

check.q: Which sentence uses a rhetorical question well?
options: Surely a little fresh air is a small price for a calmer morning?
check.why: C is a controlled rhetorical question that supports the argument. A is a fact; B is overdone and over-punctuated.

teach.note: Mini-whiteboards. The answer is C. A is a fact; B overuses devices without sense.

teach.heading: Proofreading for AO6
bullets: Check capitals, full stops and comma splices.
Check apostrophes (its / it's; children's).
Check spelling of tricky words (separate, definitely).
Read the final paragraph aloud in your head.
teach.note: Remind pupils that 16 marks are for technical accuracy. Teach a 'last five minutes' routine.

practice: Write one rhetorical question and one triplet for your own article.
Write a counter-argument sentence starting 'Admittedly'.
Proofread two sentences with three planted errors.
independent: Core: Write one body paragraph with three devices from A-F-O-R-E-S-T.
Extend: Write two body paragraphs with a counter-argument and a link back.
Stretch: Complete the 400-word article and annotate five techniques.
exit: Name three persuasive techniques.
Why must a counter-argument be answered?
Big question: when do techniques become too much?
lessons.homework: Write the final paragraph (a call to action) for the article and proofread it using the last-five-minutes routine.
lessons.send: SEND: give a technique card with example sentences; allow a phrase bank for sign-posting (firstly, however, finally). EAL/international: pre-teach 'rhetorical', 'triplet', 'emotive', 'admittedly'; idioms 'to have the last word', 'food for thought'; stems: 'Surely ...?', 'Admittedly ... but ...', 'It is time to ...'. Cultural note: UK persuasive writing uses understated humour and rhetorical questions; avoid insults. Stretch: construct a speech version with repetition and direct address.

lessons.unit: SL: Spoken Language endorsement (AO7 to AO9)
lessons.title: Spoken Language: planning a formal presentation
lessons.bigQuestion: How do I plan a talk that is clear, interesting and mine?
objectives: Choose a presentation topic and purpose that you can explain with authority
Plan a presentation of up to ten minutes with a clear structure
Prepare an opening and a closing that hold the audience's attention
successCriteria: All: choose a topic and three main points
Most: plan an introduction, a sequence of points and a conclusion with evidence
Some: shape the talk with a hook, signposting, varied techniques and anticipated questions
lessons.crossCurricular: All subjects: oral communication; Citizenship: public speaking
lessons.smsc: Moral and social: truthfulness (sidq), respect for the audience and courtesy in answering questions

keywords.def: a prepared formal talk
formal grammar and vocabulary, not an accent
words that guide the audience through the talk
an opening that grabs attention
the people listening

starter: Bismillah. Retrieval: name three features of a good opening in writing.
What are the three AOs for spoken language?
Name a topic you could talk about for five minutes with real knowledge.

teach.heading: What the endorsement is

head: AO
Skill
Evidence
rows: Presentation skills in a formal setting
Listen and respond to questions and feedback
grammar and vocabulary suited to formal speech

teach.note: Say: Spoken Language does not count towards the 9-1 grade; it is reported separately as Pass, Merit, Distinction or Not Classified, and is teacher-assessed. Pupils must meet all the criteria for a grade. Tell pupils that the presentation lasts up to about ten minutes and includes questions. AO7: present; AO8: listen and respond; AO9: use spoken Standard English. Teacher to check the school's current assessment criteria from AQA.

teach.heading: Plan the talk

timeline.label: 1. Hook
timeline.text: a question, anecdote or fact (30 seconds)

timeline.label: 2. Aim
timeline.text: state what you will explain and why it matters

timeline.label: 3. Points
timeline.text: three main points, each with an example

timeline.label: 4. Summary
timeline.text: return to the hook and recap

teach.note: Show the shape as a timeline. Ask pupils to decide where the audience will most easily lose attention and what they will do. Say that notes should be cue cards with keywords, not full sentences.

teach.heading: Worked model: an opening

model.problem: Write the opening of a five-minute presentation on 'Why every community needs a library'.
steps: Start with a hook: a question or striking fact.
State your aim and your three points.
Use signposting: 'First ... second ... finally'.
Use formal but natural Standard English.
model.answer: Good morning, everyone. How many of you have ever found an answer in a library that the internet could not give you? Today I want to persuade you that every community needs a library, and I will do so in three steps: first, how libraries help learning; second, how they bring people together; and finally, why they matter most to those who have the least.

teach.note: Read the opening aloud with a clear voice. Underline the hook (question), the aim and the signposting. Note the Standard English forms such as 'I will explain' and the polite end. Cultural note: UK audiences expect a direct start and not a long preamble.

teach.heading: Hinge question

check.q: Which is the best use of notes in a presentation?
options: Write the whole speech and read it word for word.
Use cue cards with keywords and signposts.
Use no notes at all and improvise.
check.why: B keeps eye contact and structure. A reads flatly; C risks losing the thread.

teach.note: Mini-whiteboards. The answer is B. A is too wordy and C has no aim.

teach.heading: Choosing a topic
bullets: Choose something you can explain and defend.
Make sure the audience can learn something.
Prepare three facts or examples.
Predict two questions and prepare answers.
teach.note: Pupils choose something they know and care about, with a teacher's agreement. Remind them the topic must allow questions. Idiom: 'to know your stuff'.

practice: Write your hook, aim and three points on a single cue card.
Write two questions you expect from the audience.
Draft the final sentence of your presentation.
independent: Core: Write a five-line plan of your presentation using the five stages.
Extend: Write the full opening (80 words) in Standard English.
Stretch: Write the opening and closing and plan a visual or example that supports your main point.
exit: Name the three AOs for spoken language.
Why use cue cards rather than reading a script?
Big question: how do I plan a talk that is mine?
lessons.homework: Prepare a two-minute version of your opening and main points; record yourself and write three improvements.
lessons.send: SEND: provide a presentation plan template with sentence starters and allow a short practice with a trusted adult; consider the teacher's reasonable adjustments for speech and anxiety. EAL/international: pre-teach 'presentation', 'hook', 'signposting', 'cue card'; idiom 'to break the ice' = to ease nerves at the start; stems: 'Today I will explain ...', 'First ..., second ..., finally ...', 'Thank you for listening'. Cultural note: UK presentation style is direct and polite; an accent is fine, Standard English is about grammar. Stretch: plan a rhetorical device that frames the talk.

lessons.unit: SL: Spoken Language endorsement (AO7 to AO9)
lessons.title: Spoken Language: delivery, Standard English and answering questions
lessons.bigQuestion: How can my voice and my answers show confidence and respect?
objectives: Use voice, pace and eye contact to present with confidence
Use spoken Standard English accurately
Respond to questions and feedback clearly and courteously
successCriteria: All: speak clearly and audibly in Standard English
Most: vary pace and tone and answer questions with evidence
Some: respond to difficult questions diplomatically and build on feedback
lessons.crossCurricular: Drama: voice and presence; Citizenship: debate
lessons.smsc: Moral and social: courtesy (adab) in listening and answering

keywords.def: able to be heard clearly
able to be understood
make a point clear
speed of speaking
tactful and polite

starter: Bismillah. Retrieval: name the three parts of a presentation plan.
Say one sentence in Standard English about your topic.
Explain the difference between accent and Standard English.

teach.heading: Standard English in speech

misconception.wrong: 'I have to change my accent to speak Standard English.'
misconception.right: 'Standard English is grammar and vocabulary; I can keep my accent and say "we were" and "I did not".'

teach.note: State clearly that accent is not the issue: Standard English concerns grammar and vocabulary, and every accent is welcome. Ask pupils to correct sentences orally. Cultural note: in casual British talk many people say 'we was' or 'I ain't', but in a formal presentation we use Standard forms.

teach.heading: Delivery checklist
teach.note: Practise the checklist as a class with a one-sentence line. Ask each pupil to model one, for example pace. Remind pupils to breathe and pause after key points.

teach.heading: Worked model: answering a question

model.problem: An audience member asks: 'Libraries are old-fashioned; why not just use the internet?' Give a model answer.
steps: Thank the questioner.
Restate the question to show you listened.
Answer with a reason and an example.
Acknowledge a fair point; check they are satisfied.
model.answer: Thank you, that is a fair question. You are asking whether the internet makes libraries unnecessary. I would say not, because many people do not have a quiet place or reliable access at home, and a librarian can help you find reliable sources. The internet is useful, and I use it too, but a library offers something different. Does that answer your question?

teach.note: Read the question and answer. Show the steps: thank, clarify, answer with evidence, check. Note the model includes a polite correction and an honest 'I do not know' response, which is acceptable and shows truthfulness.

teach.heading: Hinge question

check.q: Which response to a challenging question is best?
options: 'Thank you; that is a fair point. I would answer that ...'
check.why: B is courteous and engages with the question. A is rude; C avoids the question.

teach.note: Mini-whiteboards. The answer is B. A dismisses the questioner; C avoids the question.

teach.heading: Feedback and AO8
bullets: Listen to the whole question first.
Pause, then answer.
Accept feedback politely; use it.
Ask for clarification when needed.
teach.note: Say that listening matters as much as speaking: AO8 asks you to respond to questions and feedback. Idiom: 'to take on board' = to accept and use feedback.

practice: Say your opening sentence in Standard English with clear pace.
Answer a partner's question using the four-step model.
Correct five spoken non-standard sentences orally.
independent: Core: Present your two-minute opening to a partner and answer two questions.
Extend: Present for four minutes with a hook and signposting; note your partner's feedback.
Stretch: Present for five minutes, answer three questions and write a short reflection on feedback.
exit: Is Standard English an accent? Explain.
Name two features of confident delivery.
Big question: how can voice and answers show confidence and respect?
lessons.homework: Practise your full presentation twice and write one improvement target for each of voice, pace and language.
lessons.send: SEND: allow additional preparation time, cue cards in large print and a small audience; reasonable adjustments to be agreed with the SENCo. EAL/international: pre-teach 'audible', 'intelligible', 'clarify', 'diplomatic'; idiom 'to take on board'; stems: 'Thank you for your question', 'What I mean is ...', 'Does that answer your question?'. Cultural note: in British settings it is polite to thank a questioner and to disagree gently. Stretch: field a hostile question without raising your voice.

lessons.unit: P2-A-Q3: Paper 2 Section A: Question 3, language
lessons.title: Paper 2 Question 3: terminology that supports analysis, never replaces it
lessons.bigQuestion: When does a technical term help my answer, and when does it hide a gap?
objectives: Use terminology to support analysis of a non-fiction writer's language
Follow each term with an explanation of effect and purpose
Spot and repair answers that rely on labels alone
successCriteria: All: name a feature and quote it accurately
Most: explain the effect on the reader and link it to the writer's viewpoint
Some: weave terms into a developed analysis of tone and purpose
lessons.crossCurricular: Media: how advertising and journalism shape readers' attitudes
lessons.smsc: Social: recognising how language can influence communities

keywords.def: words chosen to provoke feelings
speaking to the reader as 'you'
a number used as evidence
the writer's attitude, such as urgent or sarcastic
the writer's opinion or perspective

starter: Bismillah. What is the effect of the word 'crisis' compared with 'problem'?
Name two language features common in newspaper articles.
Retrieval: how many marks is Paper 2 Question 3?

teach.heading: What stays the same, what changes
bullets: Question 3 is 12 marks on one source
It tests how the writer uses language (AO2)
Terminology supports effect; it does not replace it
Non-fiction adds purpose: to persuade, inform or argue
teach.note: Link back to the Year 10 lesson: the skill is the same as Paper 1 Question 2. The difference is the text type. In non-fiction, examiners reward links to the writer's viewpoint and purpose. Check the specimen paper for the mark total (12) and the exact stem.

teach.heading: The extract

quote.text: Every morning, thousands of us crawl through the same choking traffic and call it normal. It is not normal. It is a daily waste of our lives, our money and our patience. Isn't it time somebody said enough?

teach.note: Read in a frustrated voice. Pre-teach 'choking' (making breathing hard), 'patience' (ability to wait calmly). Ask pupils which words they would underline. This extract is an original teacher-written text, not from any exam board.

teach.heading: Model: a paragraph where terms serve effect

model.problem: How does the writer use language to show frustration with traffic? (12 marks)
steps: Quote: 'crawl through the same choking traffic'. Name: emotive verb and adjective.
Effect: 'crawl' makes commuters seem helpless and slow; 'choking' suggests suffocation.
Link to viewpoint: the writer wants readers to see the problem as a daily harm.
Second quote: 'our lives, our money and our patience'. Name: tricolon with the inclusive 'our'.
Effect: it builds the cost of traffic and makes the reader feel part of the group.
model.answer: The writer uses emotive language, 'crawl through the same choking traffic', to present commuters as helpless. The verb 'crawl' suggests painfully slow movement, while 'choking' implies suffocation, so the reader feels that traffic is harmful, not merely annoying. The tricolon 'our lives, our money and our patience' builds a sense of accumulating loss, and the repeated 'our' includes the reader in a shared grievance. This persuades the reader that frustration is justified and that action is overdue.

teach.note: Colour-code terms in blue and effect in green. Point out the final sentence linking back to purpose: to persuade. Ask pupils whether the paragraph would work with no terms at all. Mostly yes, which proves that effect is the core.

teach.heading: Common error

misconception.wrong: 'The writer uses a rhetorical question, emotive language and a tricolon.'
misconception.right: 'The rhetorical question "Isn't it time somebody said enough?" invites the reader to agree, so the writer's demand for action feels like common sense.'

teach.note: The left version is a list of labels, with no quotation and no effect: it would stay in the lower levels. Ask pupils to say what is missing: evidence, effect and link to purpose.

teach.heading: Hinge question

check.q: Which sentence best shows terminology supporting analysis?
options: The writer uses direct address, a rhetorical question and statistics.
The direct address 'our lives' makes the reader feel personally affected, which strengthens the argument.
The writer talks about traffic a lot.
check.why: B names the method, quotes it, and explains the effect on the reader and the argument. A is only a list and C does not analyse language.

teach.note: Mini-whiteboards. If pupils choose A, ask: what would an examiner be able to credit besides the labels?

practice: Write one sentence on the effect of 'crawl', using the term 'verb'.
Rewrite 'The writer uses a rhetorical question' so that it explains effect.
Choose the best term for 'It is not normal. It is a daily waste': say why it works.
independent: Core: Write a four-sentence paragraph on the first two sentences, using one term and a clear effect.
Extend: Write a six-sentence paragraph using three different features and linking to purpose.
Stretch: Rewrite your paragraph with no terminology at all and compare which version is stronger.
exit: Complete: 'A term is useful when it ...'
Write one sentence on the effect of 'choking'.
Big question: when does terminology help, and when does it hide a gap?
lessons.homework: Find a short opinion piece or letter in a newspaper or magazine, copy two sentences and write a Question 3 style analysis of each, with one term and one effect.
lessons.send: SEND: provide a three-column frame: quotation, feature, effect. EAL/international: pre-teach 'choking', 'grievance', 'inclusive', 'tricolon'; stems: 'This makes the reader feel ...', 'The writer wants us to ...'. Stretch: analyse tone shifts between the three sentences.

lessons.unit: P2-B-Q5: Paper 2 Section B: Question 5, viewpoint writing
lessons.title: Paper 2 Question 5: presenting your own view on a statement linked to Section A
lessons.bigQuestion: How do I turn the ideas in Section A into my own convincing viewpoint?
objectives: Take a clear position on a statement or theme linked to Section A
Build one extended piece of writing around your own view
Use Section A ideas as support for your view, not as a summary
successCriteria: All: state a clear viewpoint in the opening
Most: develop three connected paragraphs of your own reasoning
Some: weave in Section A ideas to extend and challenge your view
lessons.crossCurricular: Citizenship: expressing a reasoned opinion on public issues
lessons.smsc: Moral: respecting different views while arguing your own

keywords.def: your own opinion, supported by reasons
the claim you respond to
your main argument in one sentence
an opposing point that you answer

starter: Bismillah. Give an opinion on 'Learning is better outdoors', with one reason.
Name one persuasive technique and use it in a sentence.
Retrieval: how many marks is Paper 2 Question 5, and how are they split?

teach.heading: What the task asks
bullets: One extended piece, worth 40 marks
You present your own view on a statement or theme
The theme links to the Section A sources
Audience, purpose and form are stated in the task
teach.note: Make clear this is a writing task, not a reading task: Question 5 sits in Section B. The statement and theme are linked to the Section A topic, but the argument must be pupils' own. 24 marks are for content and organisation and 16 for technical accuracy. The form (article, letter, speech) is given in the task, so check it.

teach.heading: Example task

quote.text: 'Children today spend too much time indoors and too little time outside.' Write an article for a local newspaper in which you present your own view on this statement.

teach.note: This is an original task in the style of the specimen paper. Real papers link to the Section A theme. Ask pupils for first reactions: agree, disagree or partly. Stress that all three positions can score fully if argued well.

teach.heading: Model: from statement to plan

model.problem: Plan a response to the task above using your own view, drawing on Section A ideas as support.
steps: Thesis: partly agree: screens are fine, but outdoor time is vital.
Paragraph 1: health and energy; use a Section A idea on activity as support.
Paragraph 2: concentration and mood; use personal experience.
Paragraph 3: counter-argument: online life also teaches skills; then answer it.
Conclusion: call to action for families and schools.
model.answer: Thesis: 'Children are not doomed by screens, but they are quietly missing something that no device can supply: fresh air.' Opening hook: 'Look out of the window. When did you last see a child out there?' Then follow the five-step plan, tying any Section A idea to your own reasoning.

teach.note: Emphasise: the Section A material may be used, but as the pupil's own view of it, for example 'As the writer of Source A observes, ...' followed by agreement or challenge. Never summarise the source for its own sake. Point out the hook, thesis and call to action.

teach.heading: Common error

misconception.wrong: Spending a paragraph retelling what Source A says about outdoor play.
misconception.right: Using one short idea from Source A as evidence, then adding your own reasoning: 'I would go further: ...'

teach.note: The task rewards your viewpoint. Retelling earns little. Ask: how could this pupil turn the retelling into support? By adding 'which is why I believe ...'.

teach.heading: Hinge question

check.q: Which opening best presents the writer's own view?
options: Source A says that children play outside less than they used to.
I believe children need more fresh air than screens can ever offer, and I will explain why.
This article is about children and the outdoors.
check.why: B states a clear personal viewpoint. A summarises a source and C describes the article without taking a position.

teach.note: Mini-whiteboards. Ask pupils to underline the words that signal a personal viewpoint ('I believe').

practice: Write a one-sentence thesis for the task, choosing your own position.
Write one sentence that uses a Section A style idea (for example, 'research suggests outdoor play improves mood') as support, without summarising.
Draft a counter-argument and one sentence answering it.
independent: Core: Write a plan with a thesis, three paragraph topics and a conclusion.
Extend: Write the first two paragraphs of your article.
Stretch: Write a counter-argument paragraph that concedes a point but still strengthens your own view.
exit: What does 'own view' mean in Question 5?
Write a hook sentence for your article.
Big question: how can Section A support your view without taking it over?
lessons.homework: Write a complete 250-word article for the task, then highlight your thesis, one counter-argument and your call to action.
lessons.send: SEND: provide a structure grid (hook, thesis, three points, answer to counter-argument, conclusion). EAL/international: pre-teach 'statement', 'counter-argument', 'concede'; stems: 'I strongly believe that ...', 'Some people argue ..., but ...'. Stretch: adapt the same view for a speech and note which techniques change.

lessons.unit: SL: Spoken Language endorsement (AO7 to AO9)
lessons.title: Spoken Language endorsement: how it is graded and reported
lessons.bigQuestion: If the endorsement carries no marks, why does it still matter?
objectives: Explain that the endorsement is graded Pass, Merit or Distinction on a competency basis
Understand that all criteria for a grade must be met
Know that it is reported separately and does not count towards the GCSE grade
successCriteria: All: name the three possible outcomes
Most: explain what 'competency basis' means
Some: explain how a single unmet criterion affects the grade, and why the endorsement is reported separately
lessons.crossCurricular: PSHE: speaking confidently, preparing for interviews
lessons.smsc: Social: speaking respectfully and listening to others

keywords.def: a separate recognition on your certificate
you must show each skill required, not collect marks
the three graded outcomes
the listed things you must demonstrate

starter: Bismillah. What is the difference between earning marks and meeting criteria?
Retrieval: what are the length and the audience for the formal presentation?
Retrieval: which skill does AO9 focus on?

teach.heading: A separate endorsement
bullets: Spoken Language is assessed by your teacher
Graded: Pass, Merit or Distinction
Reported separately on the certificate
Carries no marks and no weighting in the GCSE grade
teach.note: Make this the first clear message: it does not change the GCSE English Language grade (1 to 9). It appears separately on the certificate. Pupils often assume it gives extra marks; it does not. Stress that employers and colleges may still value it as evidence of speaking skill.

teach.heading: Competency, not marks

left.title: A mark-based paper
points: Weakness in one area can be offset

right.title: A competency endorsement
points: Each criterion is either met or not yet met
Strength elsewhere cannot cancel a gap
Every criterion for a grade must be met

teach.note: Use a driving-test analogy: you must show all required skills, not collect enough points. Check the exact wording of the criteria in AQA's current guidance (verify), because the criteria cover presenting (AO7), responding to questions and feedback (AO8) and Standard English (AO9).

teach.heading: Model: reaching a grade

model.problem: Tariq meets all the Distinction criteria except one: his answers to audience questions are brief and hesitant. All other Merit criteria are met. What grade does he get?
steps: Check every criterion for Distinction.
Notice that one criterion is not yet met.
Apply the rule: all criteria for a grade must be met.
Move to the next grade and check all of its criteria.
model.answer: Tariq is awarded Merit, because all Merit criteria are met but not every Distinction criterion. Strength elsewhere cannot make up for the unmet criterion.

teach.note: This applies the competency rule from the specification (verify wording with AQA's current published criteria). Ask: what could Tariq practise to reach Distinction next time? Answer: rehearse questions and give fuller responses. Note this is a worked example, not a real student.

teach.heading: Common error

misconception.wrong: 'Spoken Language will lower my GCSE grade if I do badly.'
misconception.right: It is graded separately and carries no marks or weighting in the GCSE English Language grade.

teach.note: Reassure anxious pupils. Equally, correct the opposite error: 'It does not matter, so I will not prepare.' A strong Distinction shows real communication skill, and the teacher can only grade what you show.

teach.heading: Hinge question

check.q: Which statement about the endorsement is correct?
options: It adds up to 20 marks towards the GCSE grade
It is reported separately and carries no marks
It is graded 9 to 1 like the written papers
check.why: It is graded Pass, Merit or Distinction, reported separately on the certificate, with no marks and no weighting in the GCSE grade.

teach.note: Mini-whiteboards. Ask pupils who chose A where the idea came from, then correct it.

practice: Write the three possible outcomes in order from lowest to highest.
Explain 'competency basis' in one sentence of your own.
Is the endorsement included when the GCSE grade is calculated? Answer in one sentence.
independent: Core: Make a small poster explaining how the endorsement works, using three bullets.
Extend: Write a paragraph advising a nervous friend about what the endorsement does and does not affect.
Stretch: Explain why a competency model is a fair way of recognising speaking skills.
exit: Name the three grades.
True or false: the endorsement changes your GCSE grade. Explain.
Big question: why does it still matter even though it carries no marks?
lessons.homework: Write a one-paragraph plan for your presentation naming the topic, one skill you will practise, and one question you expect from the audience.
lessons.send: SEND: provide a one-page visual summary with icons for Pass, Merit, Distinction and a tick-list of criteria. EAL/international: pre-teach 'endorsement', 'competency', 'criteria', 'weighting'; keep sentences short: 'It does not change my GCSE grade.' Stretch: compare this endorsement with another vocational award you know.

lessons.title: Baseline feedback: the 4EB1 paper, my targets and the short reading questions
lessons.bigQuestion: Where are my marks on the 3-hour paper, and how do I win the short ones every time?
objectives: To understand how the 4EB1 paper is built and where my own marks were lost in the baseline paper
successCriteria: All: name the three sections, their marks and their assessment objectives
Most: answer 1- and 2-mark questions with precise, brief evidence
Some: set two personal targets from an error analysis of my baseline paper
lessons.smsc: Social: honest self-assessment and setting targets with a teacher

keywords.def: the skill a question is marking (AO1 to AO5)
find and write down a fact from the text
sorting your mistakes to see their causes
the one thing you will do better next time

hook.text: If you had to give up 10 marks somewhere on the 3-hour paper, where would you least mind losing them, and why?

A clock face, for timing the paper

teach.heading: The paper at a glance
teach.note: Paper map from the specification and recent mark schemes. Section A: Questions 1 to 7 on Text One and Text Two. Section B: Question 8, directed writing that uses both texts. Section C: one task from Questions 9 to 11. Ask: which two questions carry the most reading marks? (Q7, then Q3 and Q6.)

teach.heading: Error analysis: why marks were lost
teach.note: Pupils have their marked baseline paper. Sort each lost mark into a column on the target sheet. Most lost marks fall into a few causes; naming the cause tells you the fix. Answers: 'quoted a whole paragraph' = misread; 'ran out of time for Section C' = timing; 'feature spotting' = skill; 'comma splices' = accuracy.

cards: Quoted a whole paragraph for 1 mark
Named a simile but gave no effect
Wrote about Text Two for a Text One question

teach.heading: Short questions: precise and brief
teach.note: Text One in full: teacher-written for TGA, so it may be shown in full (also on the pupil PDF). Read it aloud once. Model on paragraph 1: 'Give one thing the writer notices about the harbour (1 mark).' A precise answer: it smelled of diesel (or wet rope). No need for a sentence of explanation. For a 2-mark 'give two' question, give two separate points on two lines.

quote.text:
The harbour smelled of diesel and wet rope. The ferry was forty minutes late, and the six of us waiting on the slipway had stopped pretending to read. A gull stood on a bollard and stared at us as though we owed it money.

When we finally cast off, the sea was the colour of wet slate, and it moved like something breathing in its sleep. Each wave lifted the bow, held it, and let it drop, as if the sea were weighing us and could not decide. Nobody spoke. The engine spoke for all of us.

Halfway across, the light went. The mainland behind us shrank to a smudge; ahead there was nothing at all. I gripped the rail and thought, absurdly, of my own kitchen: the kettle, the clock, the ordinary safety I had been so keen to escape.

Then, quite suddenly, the island was there: a low grey line, then a single lamp, then a door opening. Someone on the quay was holding out a hand. I have travelled a long way since, but I have never been so grateful to arrive anywhere.
quote.source: Text One, 'The Last Ferry' (teacher-written modern travel memoir for TGA)

teach.heading: Hinge
teach.note: Poll.

check.q: 'From paragraph 1, give one detail that shows the waiting has been long.' Best answer?
options: They had stopped pretending to read.
A gull stood on a bollard.
check.why: Stopping 'pretending to read' shows boredom after a long wait; the other details are true but do not answer the focus.

practice.q: Read Text One (pupil PDF). Give one thing the writer compares the sea to in paragraph 2 (1 mark).
practice.a: Something breathing in its sleep (or: the colour of wet slate).
practice.model: Underline the focus (paragraph 2, compares). Scan only that paragraph. Write the detail, nothing more: 'Something breathing in its sleep.'

practice.q: Give two things the writer thinks about when the light goes (2 marks).
practice.a: Any two: her kitchen; the kettle; the clock; the ordinary safety she wanted to escape.

independent.q: Core: complete the error analysis sheet for your baseline paper, then write two targets in the portal response box. Starter: 'In Section ___ I lost marks because... Next time I will...'
independent.a: Two specific targets tied to a cause, e.g. 'In Q3 I named techniques without effects; I will write one effect sentence for every quotation.'
independent.model: Teacher models with an anonymous answer: cause = Q7 discussed Text One only; target = 'Every Q7 paragraph will mention both texts and use a comparative connective.'

independent.q: Extend: rank your three weakest questions by the marks they are worth.
independent.a: Highest-mark weaknesses first (usually Q7, Q8, Section C).

independent.q: Stretch: plan how you would split 180 minutes across the paper.
independent.a: For example: reading 15, Section A 60, Section B 50, Section C 50, final check 5.

exit.q: Which question compares both texts?
exit.a: C) Q7

exit.q: Answer the ponder in one sentence.
exit.a: For example: the 1-mark questions, because they are worth least; but they are also the easiest to secure, so it is better not to lose any.

lessons.homework: Learn the paper map (sections, questions, marks, AOs) for a quiz next lesson; reread Text One twice.
lessons.send: SEND: pre-filled error analysis sheet with columns. EAL: AO glossary with examples. Stretch: write a model 2-mark answer for a partner.

lessons.title: Section A language: analysing a writer's words in Text One
lessons.bigQuestion: How does a writer's choice of words make me feel what they felt?
objectives: To explain how a writer's language choices create effects on the reader in an unseen text
successCriteria: All: select short, precise quotations
Most: explain the connotations of a key word and its effect
Some: link several language choices to the writer's overall feeling

keywords.def: the ideas or feelings a word suggests
a comparison using 'like' or 'as'
giving a thing human actions or feelings
what the words make the reader think or feel

hook.text: 'The sea was the colour of wet slate.' What does 'slate' make you feel that 'grey' does not?

pictures.alt: The bow of a ferry rising on a wave

teach.heading: Zoom in on one word
teach.note: Model the thinking aloud. 'Slate' suggests cold, hard, heavy and dull; 'wet' adds chill and danger. The sea feels solid and threatening rather than beautiful. Then pupils try 'weighing'.

teach.heading: Language that makes the sea alive
teach.note: Paragraph 2 of Text One. Ask: what kind of creature is the sea here? (A sleeping animal; it could wake.) Then: what does 'weighing us' suggest? (The sea is judging the passengers, as if deciding their fate.)

quote.text: it moved like something breathing in its sleep. Each wave lifted the bow, held it, and let it drop, as if the sea were weighing us and could not decide.
quote.source: Text One, 'The Last Ferry' (teacher-written for TGA), paragraph 2

teach.heading: Model: a language paragraph
teach.note: I do. Labelled: What (method), Evidence, Effect (with connotation), Writer's purpose. Avoid 'this makes the reader want to read on'.

model.problem: How does the writer use language to show the experience of the crossing?
steps: What: the writer personifies the sea as a living creature
Evidence: 'breathing in its sleep' and 'weighing us'
Effect: 'sleep' suggests it could wake at any moment, so the calm feels fragile
Zoom: 'weighing' makes the sea a judge deciding the passengers' fate
Purpose: the reader shares the writer's sense of powerlessness
model.answer: The writer personifies the sea as a sleeping creature that 'could not decide' whether to spare them, so the reader feels the passengers' powerlessness.

teach.heading: Hinge
teach.note: Poll.

check.q: Which comment on 'Nobody spoke. The engine spoke for all of us.' is strongest?
options: The short sentences and the personified engine show a tense silence in which only the machine has a voice.
It is personification which is effective.
It makes the reader want to read on.
check.why: It names the method and explains the effect; the others feature-spot or use an empty phrase.

practice.q: Explain the effect of 'the ordinary safety I had been so keen to escape' (paragraph 3).
practice.a: Irony: the writer now longs for the safety she once found boring, which shows how frightened she is.
practice.model: Method: contrast and irony. Evidence: 'ordinary safety' against 'keen to escape'. Effect: the dull home she fled now seems precious; fear has changed her values.

practice.q: Find one word in paragraph 4 that changes the mood, and explain why.
practice.a: 'grateful' (or 'lamp', 'opening'): relief and warmth replace fear.

independent.q: Core: in the portal response box, write two language paragraphs: 'How does the writer use language to show the experience of the crossing?' Starter: 'The writer presents the sea as...'
independent.a: Two paragraphs, each with a method, a short quotation, the connotations of a key word and the effect on the reader.
independent.model: Teacher goes through paragraph 1 with the class (the sleeping-creature personification above), then pupils write paragraph 2 alone, for example on the kitchen, kettle and clock as symbols of safety.

independent.q: Extend: add one sentence on how the language changes from paragraph 2 to paragraph 4.
independent.a: It moves from threat ('weighing us') to welcome ('a door opening').

independent.q: Stretch: explain an alternative reading of 'stared at us as though we owed it money'.
independent.a: Humour that eases tension, or a hint that even nature is unfriendly to the travellers.

exit.q: A connotation is...
exit.a: A) what a word suggests

exit.q: Answer the ponder.
exit.a: 'Slate' adds hardness, cold and heaviness; the sea feels solid and threatening, not just a colour.

lessons.homework: Pick three words from Text One and write the connotations of each in a word web.
lessons.send: SEND: paragraph frame with sentence starters. EAL: glossary of 'slipway', 'bollard', 'bow', 'quay'. Stretch: analyse two methods in one sentence.

teach.note: Read aloud slowly. Teacher-written in a nineteenth-century style for TGA, so it may be shown in full. Pupils underline any phrase they cannot translate. Glossary: steam-packet (a passenger steamship), drawing-room (a comfortable sitting room), sparingly (a little), mislay (lose), embarked (got on board).

quote.text:
Let no traveller suppose that the sea will consult his convenience. She keeps her own hours, and the steam-packet, for all its iron and its puffing confidence, keeps them too. Patience is the first article of a traveller's luggage, and the last he should ever mislay.

The gentleman who complains loudly of the weather has mistaken a steamer for a drawing-room. Let him rather take a place near the middle of the vessel, where the motion is least; let him eat sparingly, keep the fresh air upon his face, and fix his eye upon the horizon, which is the only steady thing in the world on such a day.

Above all, let him observe his fellow passengers. He will learn more of mankind in one rough crossing than in a whole season of fine dinners: who is brave, who is kind, and who, at the first lurch, forgets every other soul aboard and thinks only of himself.

The sea, in short, is a stern schoolmaster; but those who attend to his lessons come ashore better travellers than they embarked.
quote.source: Text Two, 'Advice to Those Who Travel by Sea' (teacher-written in a nineteenth-century style for TGA)

Effect: the reader is warned, but gently mocked for expecting comfort
Development: the 'stern schoolmaster' metaphor turns hardship into education
model.answer: The writer presents his advice with the confident authority of experience, using formal imperatives and the metaphor of a 'stern schoolmaster' to show that hardship teaches.

objectives: To understand how to choose the right Section C task and plan a balanced discursive essay
successCriteria: All: choose the task that suits my strengths
Most: plan points for both sides with evidence
Some: reach a reasoned conclusion that answers the statement

islamicLink.text: The Qur'an teaches courteous, reasoned discussion: 'Invite to the way of your Lord with wisdom and good instruction, and argue with them in a way that is best' (an-Nahl 16:125). A good discursive essay does the same: it weighs the other side fairly and persuades with reasons, not insults.

keywords.def: writing that discusses different sides of an issue
the opposing view
your reasoned reply to the opposing view
your final, reasoned judgement

hook.text: 'Travel teaches more than any classroom.' Agree or disagree? Give one reason before the lesson starts.

pictures.alt: A signpost pointing in several directions

teach.heading: Choosing in two minutes
teach.note: Section C: one task from a choice of three (Questions 9 to 11), 30 marks: AO4 20, AO5 10. The choices usually include a discursive or argument task and imaginative tasks (narrative or descriptive); check the paper's wording. Choose the task you can plan fastest and sustain best, not the one that looks easiest.

head: Task type
Choose it if...
Watch out for...
rows: you can think of points on both sides quickly
you can see a clear shape: start, problem, change
you can picture one place in detail

teach.heading: Both sides, then a judgement
teach.note: Plan for 'Travel teaches more than any classroom.' Pupils add one point each side.

left.title: For
points: Problems must be solved on the spot

right.title: Against
points: Classrooms give knowledge travel cannot: maths, science
Travel is costly; not everyone can go
Learning needs reflection and a teacher

teach.heading: Model: a counter-argument and rebuttal paragraph
teach.note: I do. Label point, evidence, explain, develop, link (PEEDL), then the rebuttal.

model.problem: 'Travel teaches more than any classroom.' Discuss.
steps: Counter-argument: some argue a classroom gives knowledge travel cannot
Evidence: nobody learns algebra or chemistry from a train window
Concede: this is true; schools build foundations
Rebuttal: but character, patience and independence are learned by doing
Link: the best learning combines both, which answers the statement
model.answer: Some argue that a classroom gives knowledge no journey can: nobody learns algebra from a train window. That is true, and schools build the foundations. Yet patience, independence and courage are learned only by doing, which is why the wisest learners need both.

teach.heading: Hinge
teach.note: Poll.

check.q: Which conclusion is most effective?
options: Travel cannot replace the classroom, but it teaches what the classroom cannot: so the statement is half true, and both are needed.
I have run out of time.
Some people like travel and some do not.
check.why: It gives a clear, reasoned judgement on the statement; the others are vague or empty.

practice.q: Write a thesis sentence for 'Travel teaches more than any classroom.'
practice.a: For example: 'Travel teaches lessons no classroom can, but it cannot replace one; the statement is only half true.'
practice.model: State your overall view and hint at the balance: 'X, but Y; therefore...'.

practice.q: Write one 'for' point with a specific example.
practice.a: For example: 'A missed connection teaches you to ask for help and solve problems alone.'

independent.q: Core: in the portal response box, plan the whole discursive essay (introduction with thesis, two 'for' paragraphs, one counter-argument and rebuttal paragraph, conclusion), then write the introduction in full. Starter: 'Many people believe...'
independent.a: A complete plan with both sides and a reasoned judgement, plus a clear introduction.
independent.model: Teacher plans the introduction and paragraph 1 aloud with the class before pupils continue.

independent.q: Extend: write the counter-argument and rebuttal paragraph.
independent.a: A paragraph that concedes fairly and replies with reasons.

independent.q: Stretch: add a rhetorical device (rule of three, question or anecdote) to your introduction.
independent.a: A purposeful device that suits a discursive register.

exit.q: A rebuttal is...
options: your reply to the other side
exit.a: A) your reply to the other side

exit.q: Answer the ponder, now with a counter-argument.
exit.a: For example: travel teaches patience and courage, although the classroom teaches knowledge that travel cannot.

lessons.homework: Write one more paragraph of the discursive essay, using PEEDL.
lessons.send: SEND: discursive planner with boxes. EAL: discursive phrase bank ('Some argue...', 'However...'). Stretch: plan a second statement in five minutes.

lessons.title: Section C: narrative and descriptive craft for 30 marks
lessons.bigQuestion: How do I make a reader see, hear and feel a moment?
objectives: To understand how to shape a short narrative or description and craft sentences for effect
successCriteria: All: plan a narrative with a clear beginning, turning point and ending
Most: use sensory detail and varied sentences for effect
Some: control pace by zooming in on one moment

keywords.def: a story with events and change
writing that paints one place or moment
how fast or slow the writing feels
what you see, hear, smell, touch, taste

hook.text: A story called 'The Crossing'. What is being crossed? Think beyond rivers and seas.

pictures.alt: A stone bridge over a misty river
A harbour with boats in winter

resources: Tarbiyyah Secondary English scheme of work 2026-27, Year 11 HT1 English Language scheme (narrative and descriptive writing frameworks), mapped to 4EB1
Pearson Edexcel International GCSE English Language B (4EB1) specification and sample assessment materials
Narrative shape planner and descriptive senses grid (pupil PDF)

starter.a: A) both sides and a judgement

starter.q: AO4 in Section C is worth...

starter.a: A) slip into a long story

teach.heading: A shape that fits 45 minutes
teach.note: Most weak narratives have too many events. Five beats are enough. Example for 'The Crossing': a boy must cross a busy city to bring medicine to his grandmother.

timeline.label: Hook
timeline.text: Open in the moment, not with waking up

teach.heading: Pace: zoom in
teach.note: Slow the key moment with detail and short sentences; speed through travel with one sentence. Show the difference.

left.title: Fast (summary)
points: He crossed the road and reached the shop.

right.title: Slow (zoom)
points: The lights changed. A bus sighed. He stepped out.

teach.heading: Model: a descriptive opening
teach.note: I do. Original model for 'Describe a harbour in winter'. Label each method.

model.problem: Describe a harbour in winter. (30 marks)
steps: Wide shot: 'The harbour held its breath under a sky the colour of pewter.' (personification, colour)
Sound: 'Ropes knocked against masts, a slow, wooden heartbeat.' (metaphor)
Smell and touch: 'Salt stung the air; the iron rail burned with cold.'
Zoom: 'On the quay, one forgotten glove lay palm up, as if asking for something.'
Short sentence: 'Nothing moved. Then the gulls.'
model.answer: A paragraph that moves from wide to close and uses several senses and varied sentences.

teach.heading: Hinge
teach.note: Poll.

check.q: Which opening is strongest for 'The Crossing'?
options: I woke up and had breakfast.
The medicine bottle was warm in his fist, and the road in front of him roared.
This is a story about a crossing.
Once upon a time there was a boy.
check.why: It starts in the moment with a goal and a threat; the others delay or announce.

practice.q: Write three sentences that slow down one moment of crossing a busy road.
practice.a: Short sentences with precise sensory detail that stretch seconds.
practice.model: Sentence 1: one sound. Sentence 2: one movement, very short. Sentence 3: one feeling shown, not told ('His fingers tightened on the bottle.').

practice.q: Plan 'The Crossing' in five beats.
practice.a: Hook, build, turn, zoom, end, with one line each.

independent.q: Core: in the portal response box, write the opening two paragraphs of either 'The Crossing' (narrative) or 'Describe a harbour in winter' (descriptive). Starter: your own first sentence, in the moment.
independent.a: Two crafted paragraphs with sensory detail, varied sentences and controlled pace.
independent.model: Teacher goes through the descriptive model above before pupils choose and write.

independent.q: Extend: underline three sentence types you used (short, complex, fronted adverbial).
independent.a: At least three different sentence forms.

independent.q: Stretch: write an ending that echoes your opening (cyclical structure).
independent.a: An ending that returns to an image from the first line, changed.

exit.q: To slow the pace, use...
exit.a: A) short sentences and detail

exit.q: Answer the ponder with one idea.
exit.a: For example: a crossing from fear to courage, or from childhood to responsibility.

lessons.homework: Finish your narrative or description (about 400 words).
lessons.send: SEND: five-beat planner and senses grid. EAL: vocabulary bank of sounds and textures. Stretch: limit adjectives to make verbs do the work.

Most: use a range of punctuation accurately
Some: proofread and correct errors that cost marks

keywords.def: joining two sentences with only a comma (an error)
words that sound the same but differ: there, their, they're

starter.q: 'He stepped out, the bus braked.' contains...
AO5 in Section C is worth...

teach.heading: Fix the common errors
teach.note: Pupils correct each before the reveal. Answers in the notes: 1) 'He stepped out; the bus braked.' 2) 'their' 3) 'Should have'. 4) Add a paragraph break at the change of time.

cards: He stepped out, the bus braked.
They left there bags on the quay.
A story with no breaks for a page
Dialogue with no new line for a new speaker

teach.heading: The five-minute proofread
bullets: Read the last paragraph first
Full stops and capitals
Commas: no splices
Homophones: there/their, its/it's
Paragraph breaks at time, place, speaker, topic
teach.note: Reading from the end stops pupils skim-reading their own story. Corrections should be neat: one line through, the correct word above.

teach.heading: Hinge
teach.note: Poll.

check.q: Which is correctly punctuated?
options: The sea was grey, it was rough.
The sea was grey; it was rough.
The sea was grey it was rough.
the sea was grey; It was rough.
check.why: A semicolon can join two linked complete sentences; the others are a comma splice, a run-on and wrong capitals.

practice.q: Correct: 'its late, the station is empty and there train has gone.'
practice.a: It's late; the station is empty and their train has gone.
practice.model: Step 1: capital and apostrophe, 'It's'. Step 2: the comma splice becomes a semicolon. Step 3: 'there' becomes 'their' (belonging).

independent.q: Core (timed, 25 minutes): choose ONE and write it in the portal response box: (a) 'Young people spend too much time looking at screens.' Discuss. (b) Write a story called 'The Last Train Home'. (c) Describe a place you know well as night falls.
independent.a: A complete, planned response suited to the task type, with crafted sentences and accurate punctuation.
independent.model: Teacher models the two-minute choice aloud (which task can I plan fastest?) and writes a five-line plan for (c) before the timer starts.

independent.q: Extend: proofread for five minutes with the checklist; correct every error neatly.
independent.a: Errors corrected.

independent.q: Stretch: improve three sentences by changing their openings.
independent.a: Varied openings: adverbial, participle, short sentence.

exit.q: 'Their' means...
exit.a: A) belonging to them

exit.q: Answer the ponder.
exit.a: Any is fair, but run-on sentences and comma splices recur and cost the most AO5 marks.

lessons.homework: Learn the five-minute proofread; correct ten sentences on the AO5 sheet.
lessons.send: SEND: spelling list of common homophones; extra time. EAL: punctuation rules card. Stretch: use a colon, a semicolon and brackets for parenthesis correctly.

quote.text:
Three years ago I sold my car. Friends assumed I had lost my job or my mind. In fact, I had simply noticed that I was spending forty minutes a day in traffic, shouting at strangers through glass.

Now I walk the two miles to work. It takes longer, of course: thirty-five minutes in good weather, forty when the rain comes sideways off the river. But those minutes are mine. I have learned the names of the streets I used to blur past. I know which bakery opens first, which tree flowers earliest in spring, which corner smells of coffee and which of wet dogs.

Walking has not made me fitter overnight; it has made me slower, and slowness turns out to be a kind of wealth. When I arrive at my desk, my head is clear.

I am not telling you to sell your car. I am asking you to try, once a week, arriving somewhere on your own two feet. You may find, as I did, that the journey was the point.

teach.heading: Text Two (practice)
teach.note: Read aloud once; pupils annotate.

quote.text:
My dear Brother,
You ask how I bear the noise of London. I will confess a secret: I bear it by walking through it when it is asleep. Last night, being unable to rest, I set out at midnight and did not return until the milk-carts began their rounds.

The streets at that hour belong to a different nation. The gas-lamps burn with a sickly yellow patience; the river breathes a cold fog over the bridges; and every doorway seems to hold its breath. I passed a coffee-stall where three cab-men warmed their hands, and a watchman who wished me good night as gravely as a bishop.

I do not pretend the walk was wholly pleasant. My boots were soaked by the second mile, and twice I was startled by footsteps that proved to be my own echo. Yet I came home with a mind scrubbed clean.

Try it, dear Brother, when your country fields grow dull. A city at night will teach you more of your fellow men than a month of its daylight.
Your affectionate sister, Margaret

model.problem: How does the writer use language and structure to present the danger?
